About & contributing
Week 17 · Phase 4: Advanced Topics

Trustworthy Deep Learning and Theory

What it takes to trust a model, and what we do and do not understand about why deep learning works. Adversarial examples (FGSM and PGD derived, linearity explanation, threat models, adversarial training, certified defenses, transferability), distribution shift and OOD detection (max softmax, energy, Mahalanobis), uncertainty (aleatoric vs epistemic, ensembles, MC dropout, ECE, temperature scaling, conformal prediction), interpretability (saliency, SmoothGrad, Grad-CAM, Integrated Gradients, attention caveats, probing, mechanistic interpretability), fairness, privacy (membership inference, differential privacy, DP-SGD), safety and responsible release, theory highlights (randomization tests, implicit regularization, NTK, lottery tickets, grokking, double descent) and open problems. The lab attacks and defends a classifier, implements Grad-CAM, and measures calibration.

106 min read4 interactive demos14 figures23 code blocks10 exercises
Learning objectives

By the end of this week you should be able to:

  • Derive FGSM and PGD from a first-order model of the loss, explain the linearity account of adversarial vulnerability, and state precisely what a threat model is.
  • Implement adversarial training as a min-max problem, and explain why it costs more, why it trades off clean accuracy, and why certified defenses give weaker but provable guarantees.
  • Classify distribution shifts (covariate, label, concept) and implement max-softmax, energy and Mahalanobis out-of-distribution detectors.
  • Separate aleatoric from epistemic uncertainty, build deep ensembles and MC dropout, compute the expected calibration error, and fix miscalibration with temperature scaling.
  • State and prove the marginal coverage guarantee of split conformal prediction.
  • Derive Grad-CAM, SmoothGrad and Integrated Gradients (with its axioms), and explain why attention weights and probing accuracy are not explanations.
  • Describe circuits, superposition and sparse autoencoders in mechanistic interpretability.
  • Compute demographic parity and equalized odds gaps, explain why they cannot generally be satisfied together, and list mitigation strategies.
  • Define membership inference, (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta)(ε,δ)-differential privacy and DP-SGD, and reason about the privacy-utility trade-off.
  • Explain what the randomization experiments, implicit regularization, the neural tangent kernel, the lottery ticket hypothesis, grokking and double descent each tell us (and do not tell us) about generalization.

For seventeen weeks the question was "how do I get a network to minimize a loss on a dataset". This week the question is "should anyone rely on the result". A classifier with 99% test accuracy can be fooled by a change to its input that no human notices. A medical model that is accurate on the hospital that trained it can fail at the next hospital over. A model that says "97% confident" may be right only 60% of the time. A heat map that "explains" a prediction may be the same map you would get from a network with random weights. A model trained on private records can sometimes be made to reveal them. None of these failures show up in the number you were optimizing, which is why this material matters: test accuracy under the training distribution is a necessary condition for a good model and a very weak sufficient one.

The second half of the week turns around and asks the theorist's question: why does any of this work at all? Classical learning theory says a model with more parameters than training points should overfit catastrophically. Modern networks interpolate their training data, including random labels, and still generalize. We will look at what is understood (a surprising amount in simplified settings), what is conjectured, and what is simply unknown.

A note on tone. Trustworthiness is a field with many results that are negative (impossibility theorems, attacks that break defenses) and many that are empirical and fragile (a saliency method that works on one network). Throughout, I will separate what is proven, what is empirical, and what is folklore.

Adversarial examples

The phenomenon

In 2013, Szegedy and colleagues reported something startling: for a trained image classifier you can find a tiny perturbation δ\boldsymbol{\delta}δ, invisible to a person, such that f(x+δ)f(\boldsymbol{x}+\boldsymbol{\delta})f(x+δ) is confidently wrong. Biggio et al. had demonstrated related evasion attacks against classical classifiers in the same period. The perturbed input is an adversarial example. It is not noise: random perturbations of the same size almost never change the prediction, yet a carefully chosen one succeeds on essentially every input of an undefended network.

History

Szegedy et al., "Intriguing properties of neural networks" (2013/2014), found adversarial examples by box-constrained L-BFGS. Goodfellow, Shlens and Szegedy, "Explaining and harnessing adversarial examples" (ICLR 2015), proposed the one-step FGSM attack and the linearity hypothesis. Madry et al., "Towards deep learning models resistant to adversarial attacks" (ICLR 2018), framed robustness as a saddle-point problem and popularized PGD adversarial training. Athalye, Carlini and Wagner (ICML 2018) showed that most defenses published at ICLR 2018 relied on "obfuscated gradients" and could be broken, a lesson that still shapes how defenses are evaluated.

Threat models

A defense is meaningless without saying what attack it defends against. A threat model specifies four things.

  1. Goal. Untargeted: make the prediction anything but the true class. Targeted: make it a chosen class ttt. Or other goals such as raising the loss, or inducing a high-confidence error.
  2. Capability (the perturbation set). Most of the literature uses an ℓp\ell_pℓp​ ball S={δ:∥δ∥p≤ϵ}\mathcal{S}=\{\boldsymbol{\delta}:\norm{\boldsymbol{\delta}}_p\le\epsilon\}S={δ:∥δ∥p​≤ϵ}, usually p=∞p=\inftyp=∞ (each pixel moves at most ϵ\epsilonϵ, typically 8/2558/2558/255 on CIFAR-10), p=2p=2p=2, or p=0p=0p=0/111 (few pixels change). The ℓp\ell_pℓp​ ball is a convenient proxy for "imperceptible", not a faithful model of real attackers: rotations, patches, colour shifts, paraphrases and prompt injections are all valid attacks outside it.
  3. Knowledge. White-box: the attacker knows weights and architecture and can compute gradients. Black-box: the attacker can only query (score-based or label-only), or only has a surrogate model (transfer attacks).
  4. Setting. Digital (edit the pixels), physical (adversarial stickers, glasses frames, printed patches that survive camera capture), training time (poisoning, backdoors) versus test time (evasion).

FGSM: the one-step attack

Let L(θ,x,y)\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta},\boldsymbol{x},y)L(θ,x,y) be the loss of a classifier with parameters θ\boldsymbol{\theta}θ at input x\boldsymbol{x}x and label yyy. Training differentiates with respect to θ\boldsymbol{\theta}θ; an attack differentiates with respect to x\boldsymbol{x}x, which you can do with the same backpropagation machinery. The attacker wants a perturbation δ\boldsymbol{\delta}δ in the allowed set that maximizes the loss. Start with the first-order Taylor expansion around x\boldsymbol{x}x:

L(θ,x+δ,y)  ≈  L(θ,x,y)+δ⊤g,g=∇xL(θ,x,y).\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta},\boldsymbol{x}+\boldsymbol{\delta},y)\;\approx\;\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta},\boldsymbol{x},y)+\boldsymbol{\delta}^\top \boldsymbol{g},\qquad \boldsymbol{g}=\nabla_{\boldsymbol{x}}\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta},\boldsymbol{x},y).L(θ,x+δ,y)≈L(θ,x,y)+δ⊤g,g=∇x​L(θ,x,y).

So within the ball of radius ϵ\epsilonϵ the attacker maximizes the linear function δ⊤g\boldsymbol{\delta}^\top\boldsymbol{g}δ⊤g. This is exactly the definition of a dual norm: max⁡∥δ∥p≤ϵδ⊤g=ϵ∥g∥q\max_{\norm{\boldsymbol{\delta}}_p\le\epsilon}\boldsymbol{\delta}^\top\boldsymbol{g}=\epsilon\norm{\boldsymbol{g}}_qmax∥δ∥p​≤ϵ​δ⊤g=ϵ∥g∥q​ with 1/p+1/q=11/p+1/q=11/p+1/q=1.

Derivation: the optimal first-order perturbation for ℓ∞\ell_\inftyℓ∞​ and ℓ2\ell_2ℓ2​

ℓ∞\ell_\inftyℓ∞​ (p=∞p=\inftyp=∞, q=1q=1q=1). The constraint is ∣δi∣≤ϵ\abs{\delta_i}\le\epsilon∣δi​∣≤ϵ for every coordinate independently, so we maximize ∑iδigi\sum_i\delta_i g_i∑i​δi​gi​ coordinatewise. Each term is largest when δi=ϵ sign(gi)\delta_i=\epsilon\,\mathrm{sign}(g_i)δi​=ϵsign(gi​). Hence δ⋆=ϵ sign(g),δ⋆⊤g=ϵ∑i∣gi∣=ϵ∥g∥1.\boldsymbol{\delta}^\star=\epsilon\,\mathrm{sign}(\boldsymbol{g}),\qquad \boldsymbol{\delta}^{\star\top}\boldsymbol{g}=\epsilon\sum_i\abs{g_i}=\epsilon\norm{\boldsymbol{g}}_1.δ⋆=ϵsign(g),δ⋆⊤g=ϵi∑​∣gi​∣=ϵ∥g∥1​. This is the Fast Gradient Sign Method: xadv=x+ϵ sign(∇xL)\boldsymbol{x}_{\text{adv}}=\boldsymbol{x}+\epsilon\,\mathrm{sign}(\nabla_{\boldsymbol{x}}\mathcal{L})xadv​=x+ϵsign(∇x​L).

ℓ2\ell_2ℓ2​ (p=2p=2p=2, q=2q=2q=2). By Cauchy-Schwarz, δ⊤g≤∥δ∥2∥g∥2≤ϵ∥g∥2\boldsymbol{\delta}^\top\boldsymbol{g}\le\norm{\boldsymbol{\delta}}_2\norm{\boldsymbol{g}}_2\le\epsilon\norm{\boldsymbol{g}}_2δ⊤g≤∥δ∥2​∥g∥2​≤ϵ∥g∥2​, with equality iff δ\boldsymbol{\delta}δ points along g\boldsymbol{g}g and has length ϵ\epsilonϵ: δ⋆=ϵ g∥g∥2.\boldsymbol{\delta}^\star=\epsilon\,\frac{\boldsymbol{g}}{\norm{\boldsymbol{g}}_2}.δ⋆=ϵ∥g∥2​g​. The ℓ2\ell_2ℓ2​ attack is simply a normalized gradient step. Note the loss increase predicted by the linear model is ϵ∥g∥1\epsilon\norm{\boldsymbol{g}}_1ϵ∥g∥1​ in the first case and ϵ∥g∥2\epsilon\norm{\boldsymbol{g}}_2ϵ∥g∥2​ in the second; since ∥g∥1\norm{\boldsymbol{g}}_1∥g∥1​ can be as large as d ∥g∥2\sqrt d\,\norm{\boldsymbol{g}}_2d​∥g∥2​, the ℓ∞\ell_\inftyℓ∞​ attack is far more powerful per unit "per-coordinate" budget in high dimension. That observation is the heart of the next subsection.

Why linearity is enough: the high-dimensional argument

Goodfellow et al. argued that adversarial examples do not require the extreme non-linearity that many assumed; they are a consequence of the near-linear behaviour of networks (ReLU, maxout and tuned sigmoids are all piecewise or locally linear) in high dimension. Consider a linear score s(x)=w⊤xs(\boldsymbol{x})=\boldsymbol{w}^\top\boldsymbol{x}s(x)=w⊤x and an ℓ∞\ell_\inftyℓ∞​ perturbation of size ϵ\epsilonϵ. The change in the score is

w⊤δ=ϵ w⊤sign(w)=ϵ∥w∥1.\boldsymbol{w}^\top\boldsymbol{\delta}=\epsilon\,\boldsymbol{w}^\top\mathrm{sign}(\boldsymbol{w})=\epsilon\norm{\boldsymbol{w}}_1.w⊤δ=ϵw⊤sign(w)=ϵ∥w∥1​.

If the weights have typical magnitude mmm per coordinate and the input has ddd dimensions, then ∥w∥1≈m d\norm{\boldsymbol{w}}_1\approx m\,d∥w∥1​≈md. The perturbation is tiny in every coordinate (ϵ\epsilonϵ), yet the score moves by ϵ m d\epsilon\,m\,dϵmd, growing linearly in the dimension. A 224 by 224 by 3 image has d≈150,000d\approx 150{,}000d≈150,000. Each pixel can move by less than the 8-bit quantization step and the logit can still move by a very large amount, because thousands of tiny aligned contributions add up. The perturbation is aligned with the weights; random noise is not, and adds up like d\sqrt dd​ rather than ddd.

The following chart is a computation, not an illustration. I trained a logistic regression on two Gaussian classes whose means differ by a fixed small amount per coordinate, in d=10d=10d=10, 100100100 and 100010001000 dimensions, and attacked it with FGSM. Higher dimension gives a more accurate clean model (more evidence is available) and also a model that collapses at a fixed ϵ\epsilonϵ-per-pixel once ϵ\epsilonϵ passes the per-coordinate signal.

The linearity explanation predicts several things that experiments confirm: adversarial examples transfer between models (similar linear structure), they exist in all directions weakly correlated with the weights rather than in isolated pockets, and training procedures that make the function more linear (like Goodfellow's early observations on shallow models) did not remove them. It is not the whole story: Ilyas et al. (2019) argued that standard datasets contain non-robust but predictive features that models legitimately use, so adversarial vulnerability is also a property of the data, and Gilmer et al. (2018) and Shafahi et al. (2019) proved that in high dimension even small-error classifiers must be vulnerable under some assumptions about the data distribution. Treat "linearity" as one correct and useful lens among several.

PGD: the iterated attack

FGSM trusts the linear model across a whole ϵ\epsilonϵ-step. If the loss curves, a better strategy is to take several small steps and re-linearize each time. Projected Gradient Descent (really gradient ascent on the loss) with random start, as used by Madry et al.:

x(0)=x+u, u∼U[−ϵ,ϵ]d,x(t+1)=ΠBϵ(x)(x(t)+α sign(∇xL(θ,x(t),y))),\boldsymbol{x}^{(0)}=\boldsymbol{x}+\boldsymbol{u},\ \boldsymbol{u}\sim U[-\epsilon,\epsilon]^d,\qquad \boldsymbol{x}^{(t+1)}=\Pi_{\mathcal{B}_\epsilon(\boldsymbol{x})}\Big(\boldsymbol{x}^{(t)}+\alpha\,\mathrm{sign}\big(\nabla_{\boldsymbol{x}}\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta},\boldsymbol{x}^{(t)},y)\big)\Big),x(0)=x+u, u∼U[−ϵ,ϵ]d,x(t+1)=ΠBϵ​(x)​(x(t)+αsign(∇x​L(θ,x(t),y))),

where Π\PiΠ projects back into the allowed set (for ℓ∞\ell_\inftyℓ∞​ this is a coordinatewise clip to [x−ϵ,x+ϵ][\boldsymbol{x}-\epsilon,\boldsymbol{x}+\epsilon][x−ϵ,x+ϵ], and also into the valid pixel range [0,1][0,1][0,1]), and α\alphaα is a step size, commonly ϵ/4\epsilon/4ϵ/4 for 10 steps or 2.5ϵ/T2.5\epsilon/T2.5ϵ/T for TTT steps. The random start matters: it avoids the case where the gradient at the clean point is uninformative (a flat region of a saturated softmax) and gives the attack access to different local maxima.

FGSM is PGD with one step, α=ϵ\alpha=\epsilonα=ϵ and no random start. PGD is considered the standard "first-order adversary": Madry et al. found that the loss values reached by many random restarts of PGD were similar, which suggests the local maxima are of comparable quality, and a defense that survives strong PGD is robust against a broad class of gradient-based attacks. Stronger evaluation uses an ensemble such as AutoAttack (Croce and Hein, 2020), which combines adaptive-step PGD variants with a margin-based loss and a black-box attack, precisely because weak attacks flatter weak defenses.

pythonattacks.py
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F


def fgsm(model, x, y, eps):
    """One-step L-infinity attack. x in [0,1], shape (B, C, H, W)."""
    x = x.clone().detach().requires_grad_(True)
    loss = F.cross_entropy(model(x), y)
    grad, = torch.autograd.grad(loss, x)          # d loss / d x, same shape as x
    x_adv = x + eps * grad.sign()
    return x_adv.clamp(0, 1).detach()


def pgd(model, x, y, eps, alpha, steps, random_start=True):
    """Iterated L-infinity attack with projection onto the eps-ball and the valid pixel range."""
    x_adv = x.clone().detach()
    if random_start:
        x_adv = (x_adv + torch.empty_like(x).uniform_(-eps, eps)).clamp(0, 1)
    for _ in range(steps):
        x_adv.requires_grad_(True)
        loss = F.cross_entropy(model(x_adv), y)
        grad, = torch.autograd.grad(loss, x_adv)
        x_adv = x_adv.detach() + alpha * grad.sign()
        x_adv = torch.min(torch.max(x_adv, x - eps), x + eps)   # project to the L-inf ball
        x_adv = x_adv.clamp(0, 1)                                # and to the image domain
    return x_adv.detach()


def pgd_l2(model, x, y, eps, alpha, steps):
    """L2 variant: normalized-gradient step, then rescale the perturbation to norm <= eps."""
    x_adv = x.clone().detach()
    for _ in range(steps):
        x_adv.requires_grad_(True)
        loss = F.cross_entropy(model(x_adv), y)
        grad, = torch.autograd.grad(loss, x_adv)
        g = grad / (grad.flatten(1).norm(dim=1).view(-1, 1, 1, 1) + 1e-12)
        x_adv = x_adv.detach() + alpha * g
        delta = x_adv - x
        norm = delta.flatten(1).norm(dim=1).view(-1, 1, 1, 1)
        delta = delta * torch.clamp(eps / (norm + 1e-12), max=1.0)
        x_adv = (x + delta).clamp(0, 1)
    return x_adv.detach()


@torch.no_grad()
def robust_accuracy(model, loader, attack, device="cpu", **kw):
    model.eval()
    correct = total = 0
    for x, y in loader:
        x, y = x.to(device), y.to(device)
        with torch.enable_grad():          # the attack needs gradients even inside a no_grad function
            x_adv = attack(model, x, y, **kw)
        correct += (model(x_adv).argmax(1) == y).sum().item()
        total += y.numel()
    return correct / total

Notice the model must be in eval() mode while attacking (so batch norm and dropout are deterministic) and that gradients are taken with respect to the input, which is why the input tensor needs requires_grad_(True) and torch.autograd.grad is cleaner than loss.backward() (which would also accumulate parameter gradients).

Adversarial training

The most reliable empirical defense is to train on adversarial examples. Madry et al. wrote robust training as a saddle-point problem:

min⁡θ  E(x,y)∼D[max⁡δ∈S L(θ,x+δ,y)].\min_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\ \ \E_{(\boldsymbol{x},y)\sim\mathcal{D}}\Big[\max_{\boldsymbol{\delta}\in\mathcal{S}}\ \mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta},\boldsymbol{x}+\boldsymbol{\delta},y)\Big].θmin​  E(x,y)∼D​[δ∈Smax​ L(θ,x+δ,y)].

The inner maximization is the attacker (approximated by PGD) and the outer minimization is the learner. Danskin's theorem says that, under mild conditions, the gradient of the inner maximum with respect to θ\boldsymbol{\theta}θ equals the gradient of the loss evaluated at the maximizer δ⋆\boldsymbol{\delta}^\starδ⋆; so we can run PGD to get δ⋆\boldsymbol{\delta}^\starδ⋆, then take an ordinary SGD step on L(θ,x+δ⋆,y)\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta},\boldsymbol{x}+\boldsymbol{\delta}^\star,y)L(θ,x+δ⋆,y). (The theorem needs exact maximization and differentiability, so for ReLU networks and approximate PGD it is a heuristic justification, though one that works.)

pythonadv_train.py
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F
from attacks import pgd


def adversarial_epoch(model, loader, opt, eps=8 / 255, alpha=2 / 255, steps=7, device="cpu"):
    """One epoch of PGD adversarial training (Madry et al., 2018)."""
    model.train()
    total_loss = total_correct = n = 0
    for x, y in loader:
        x, y = x.to(device), y.to(device)
        # inner maximization: craft the attack against the CURRENT weights.
        # (Batch norm: many implementations switch to eval() here; either way, be consistent.)
        model.eval()
        x_adv = pgd(model, x, y, eps=eps, alpha=alpha, steps=steps)
        model.train()
        # outer minimization: ordinary SGD step on the adversarial batch
        logits = model(x_adv)
        loss = F.cross_entropy(logits, y)
        opt.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)
        loss.backward()
        opt.step()
        total_loss += loss.item() * y.numel()
        total_correct += (logits.argmax(1) == y).sum().item()
        n += y.numel()
    return total_loss / n, total_correct / n

Adversarial training has well-known costs and phenomena.

  • Compute. With KKK PGD steps, each iteration costs about K+1K+1K+1 forward-backward passes, so training is roughly 8×8\times8× slower for K=7K=7K=7. Fast variants exist ("Fast is better than free", Wong, Rice and Kolter, 2020, used FGSM with a random start plus a cyclic learning rate, and Shafahi et al. 2019 recycled gradients), but single-step training can suffer catastrophic overfitting, where the model suddenly becomes robust to FGSM and loses all robustness to PGD.
  • Accuracy trade-off. On CIFAR-10 at ℓ∞\ell_\inftyℓ∞​ ϵ=8/255\epsilon=8/255ϵ=8/255, standard models reach about 95% clean accuracy and 0% robust accuracy; PGD-trained ResNets typically reach about 80-87% clean and about 45-55% robust accuracy depending on architecture and extra data. Tsipras et al. (2019) and Zhang et al. (TRADES, 2019) analysed this as an inherent tension, and TRADES adds an explicit KL term between clean and adversarial predictions to trade the two off with a weight β\betaβ.
  • Capacity and data. Robust training needs larger networks (Madry et al.) and benefits strongly from more data, including unlabeled or synthetic data (Carmon et al. 2019; Gowal et al. 2020, 2021).
  • Robust overfitting. Robust test accuracy peaks early in training and then falls while robust training accuracy keeps rising (Rice, Wong and Kolter, 2020), so early stopping on a robust validation set matters.
  • Robustness is specific. A model robust to ℓ∞\ell_\inftyℓ∞​ at 8/2558/2558/255 is not robust to ℓ2\ell_2ℓ2​ at a matching radius, nor to rotations, nor to common corruptions beyond what it saw.

Certified defenses (overview)

Empirical robustness has an uncomfortable property: "no attack I tried succeeded" proves nothing. A certified defense gives a guarantee: for input x\boldsymbol{x}x the prediction is provably constant over the whole ball ∥δ∥≤r\norm{\boldsymbol{\delta}}\le r∥δ∥≤r. Three families dominate.

  • Interval bound propagation (IBP) and convex relaxations. Propagate lower and upper bounds on each activation through the network. If the lower bound on the true-class logit minus every other upper bound is positive, the point is certified. Tighter relaxations (CROWN, linear programming, semidefinite programs) cost more. Training with the bound as the loss (Gowal et al. 2018; Wong and Kolter 2018) yields models with certified accuracy but lower clean accuracy.
  • Lipschitz-constrained networks. If every logit difference is LLL-Lipschitz in ℓ2\ell_2ℓ2​ and the margin is m=fy−max⁡j≠yfjm=f_y-\max_{j\ne y}f_jm=fy​−maxj=y​fj​, then no perturbation of norm smaller than m/(2L)m/(\sqrt2 L)m/(2​L) can change the prediction. Spectral-normalized and orthogonal layers keep LLL small by construction.
  • Randomized smoothing. Cohen, Rosenfeld and Kolter (ICML 2019) define a smoothed classifier g(x)=arg⁡max⁡c Pη∼N(0,σ2I)[f(x+η)=c]g(\boldsymbol{x})=\arg\max_c\ \P_{\boldsymbol{\eta}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2 I)}[f(\boldsymbol{x}+\boldsymbol{\eta})=c]g(x)=argmaxc​ Pη∼N(0,σ2I)​[f(x+η)=c]. If the top class has probability at least pAp_ApA​ and the runner-up at most pBp_BpB​, then ggg is constant within ℓ2\ell_2ℓ2​ radius R=σ2(Φ−1(pA)−Φ−1(pB))R=\tfrac{\sigma}{2}\big(\Phi^{-1}(p_A)-\Phi^{-1}(p_B)\big)R=2σ​(Φ−1(pA​)−Φ−1(pB​)), where Φ−1\Phi^{-1}Φ−1 is the standard normal quantile. Probabilities are estimated by Monte Carlo sampling with a confidence bound, so the certificate holds with high probability. It scales to ImageNet because it only needs black-box evaluations of fff. The price is slow inference (hundreds to thousands of samples) and certificates that are small in the ℓ∞\ell_\inftyℓ∞​ sense for high-dimensional inputs.

Certified accuracy is always below empirical robust accuracy for the same radius, because it must hold against every attack. The gap between what attacks achieve and what certificates prove is itself a measure of how much we do not know.

Transferability and black-box attacks

An adversarial example crafted against model A often fools model B, even with a different architecture or training set. Papernot, McDaniel and Goodfellow (2016) and Liu et al. (2017) showed that this enables transfer attacks: train a surrogate, attack it with white-box methods, and send the result to the victim. Transfer is stronger when the models share training data, when the surrogate is simpler (smoother), and when attacks are regularized to avoid over-fitting to the surrogate (momentum, input diversity, ensembles of surrogates). Transfer is also why "hide the weights" is not a defense. Other black-box options are score-based attacks that estimate the gradient from queried probabilities (finite differences, NES, SPSA) and decision-based attacks such as the Boundary Attack (Brendel et al. 2018) that need only the predicted label.

Gradient masking

A defense that makes gradients useless (non-differentiable preprocessing, randomization, saturating activations, shattered gradients) makes gradient attacks fail without making the model robust. Warning signs: single-step attacks beat iterative ones, black-box or transfer attacks beat white-box ones, increasing ϵ\epsilonϵ does not monotonically lower accuracy, and unbounded attacks do not reach 0%. Test with adaptive attacks (BPDA, EOT) and a standard suite such as AutoAttack.

Beyond images

The same ideas apply to text (synonym swaps, character edits, universal suffixes that jailbreak language models, Zou et al. 2023), audio, malware and reinforcement-learning policies. Discrete inputs break the gradient step, so attacks use gradient-guided search over tokens. Prompt injection, where untrusted text carries instructions to an LLM agent, is the adversarial-example problem again, but with no tidy norm ball.

Distribution shift and out-of-distribution detection

What can change

Every guarantee in supervised learning assumes the test data are drawn from the same distribution as the training data. Deployment violates this constantly. Write the joint distribution as p(x,y)=p(y∣x) p(x)=p(x∣y) p(y)p(\boldsymbol{x},y)=p(y\mid\boldsymbol{x})\,p(\boldsymbol{x})=p(\boldsymbol{x}\mid y)\,p(y)p(x,y)=p(y∣x)p(x)=p(x∣y)p(y). Different factorizations make different shifts easy to describe.

Shift What changes What stays Example Standard fix
Covariate shift p(x)p(\boldsymbol{x})p(x) p(y∣x)p(y\mid\boldsymbol{x})p(y∣x) A camera is replaced; photos are brighter Importance weighting w(x)=ptest(x)/ptrain(x)w(\boldsymbol{x})=p_{\text{test}}(\boldsymbol{x})/p_{\text{train}}(\boldsymbol{x})w(x)=ptest​(x)/ptrain​(x), augmentation, domain adaptation
Label (prior) shift p(y)p(y)p(y) p(x∣y)p(\boldsymbol{x}\mid y)p(x∣y) A disease becomes more prevalent Re-estimate class priors (BBSE, EM of Saerens et al.), re-weight the posterior

Subpopulation shift mixture weights of groups within-group distributions A face model is trained mostly on one demographic Group-robust training (Group DRO), data collection

Under covariate shift you can correct the loss: Eptest[ℓ]=Eptrain ⁣[w(x) ℓ]\E_{p_{\text{test}}}[\ell]=\E_{p_{\text{train}}}\!\big[w(\boldsymbol{x})\,\ell\big]Eptest​​[ℓ]=Eptrain​​[w(x)ℓ], provided the support of ptrainp_{\text{train}}ptrain​ covers that of ptestp_{\text{test}}ptest​ and the weights do not have exploding variance. Weights are typically estimated with a domain classifier: train a model to tell train from test inputs, then w(x)∝c(x)1−c(x)w(\boldsymbol{x})\propto \frac{c(\boldsymbol{x})}{1-c(\boldsymbol{x})}w(x)∝1−c(x)c(x)​ where ccc is its output.

Shift is not hypothetical. Benchmarks such as ImageNet-C (Hendrycks and Dietterich, 2019: 15 corruption types at 5 severities), ImageNet-A and ImageNet-R, and WILDS (Koh et al., 2021, with real shifts across hospitals, cameras and time) show that accuracy collapses under shifts that humans shrug off. A recurring empirical finding (Recht et al. 2019, Taori et al. 2020, Miller et al. 2021) is that in-distribution accuracy and out-of-distribution accuracy are strongly (often linearly, after a probit transform) correlated across many models: better models are better out of distribution too. Robustness interventions that move a model off this line, such as training on far more diverse data, as with CLIP-style models, are the rare and interesting ones.

The OOD detection problem

A related, narrower task: given an input, decide whether it comes from the training distribution (in-distribution, ID) or from something the model was not trained for (out-of-distribution, OOD). We want a score s(x)s(\boldsymbol{x})s(x) that is high on ID inputs and low on OOD inputs, thresholded to flag suspicious ones. Evaluation uses threshold-free metrics: AUROC of ID versus OOD, AUPR, and FPR@95TPR (the fraction of OOD inputs accepted when 95% of ID inputs are accepted). Choose the OOD set carefully: "CIFAR-10 versus SVHN" is easy; "CIFAR-10 versus CIFAR-100" (near-OOD) is much harder.

Max softmax probability (MSP)

The simplest baseline (Hendrycks and Gimpel, 2017) uses the classifier's own confidence: sMSP(x)=max⁡c softmax⁡(z)cs_{\text{MSP}}(\boldsymbol{x})=\max_c\,\softmax(\boldsymbol{z})_csMSP​(x)=maxc​softmax(z)c​ where z=f(x)\boldsymbol{z}=f(\boldsymbol{x})z=f(x) are the logits. It works surprisingly well, and its main failure is structural: softmax is shift-invariant and its confidence can be made arbitrarily high far from the training data (a ReLU network is piecewise linear, so scaling the input scales the logits and the softmax saturates; Hein, Andriushchenko and Bitterwolf 2019 proved this). Overconfident OOD predictions are not a bug of a particular network, they are generic.

ODIN (Liang, Li and Srikant, 2018) improves MSP with temperature scaling of the softmax and a small gradient-based input perturbation that increases the max-softmax score; the perturbation helps ID inputs more than OOD ones, widening the gap.

Energy score

Interpret the logits as defining an energy-based model: E(x;f)=−Tlog⁡∑cezc/TE(\boldsymbol{x};f)=-T\log\sum_c e^{z_c/T}E(x;f)=−Tlog∑c​ezc​/T (negative temperature-scaled log-sum-exp). The Gibbs distribution gives p(x)∝e−E(x)/Tp(\boldsymbol{x})\propto e^{-E(\boldsymbol{x})/T}p(x)∝e−E(x)/T, so low energy means high density under the model. Liu et al. (NeurIPS 2020) use senergy(x)=Tlog⁡∑cezc/Ts_{\text{energy}}(\boldsymbol{x})=T\log\sum_c e^{z_c/T}senergy​(x)=Tlog∑c​ezc​/T as the ID score. Why does it beat MSP? The softmax normalizes away the overall magnitude of the logits: MSP depends only on differences between logits, while the log-sum-exp also reflects how large the logits are in absolute terms, and ID data tend to produce larger logits. Concretely, log⁡max⁡cpc=zmax⁡−log⁡∑cezc\log\max_c p_c = z_{\max}-\log\sum_c e^{z_c}logmaxc​pc​=zmax​−log∑c​ezc​, which couples a growing numerator and a growing denominator, so the two cancel to a large extent. The energy score keeps the denominator term alone.

Mahalanobis distance

A feature-space approach (Lee et al., NeurIPS 2018) assumes that the penultimate-layer features h\boldsymbol{h}h of each class are Gaussian with class mean μc\boldsymbol{\mu}_cμc​ and a shared covariance Σ\SigmaΣ (this is the assumption behind linear discriminant analysis). The score is the negative squared Mahalanobis distance to the closest class mean:

sMaha(x)=−min⁡c (h(x)−μc)⊤Σ−1(h(x)−μc).s_{\text{Maha}}(\boldsymbol{x})=-\min_c\ (\boldsymbol{h}(\boldsymbol{x})-\boldsymbol{\mu}_c)^\top\Sigma^{-1}(\boldsymbol{h}(\boldsymbol{x})-\boldsymbol{\mu}_c).sMaha​(x)=−cmin​ (h(x)−μc​)⊤Σ−1(h(x)−μc​).

Parameters are estimated from the training features: μc\boldsymbol{\mu}_cμc​ is the class mean and Σ\SigmaΣ the within-class covariance averaged over classes. The Mahalanobis metric whitens the features, so directions with low variance (where a deviation is rare among ID data) count more than high-variance directions. It is a generative detector built on a discriminative network and it can use features from several layers. Its weakness is the Gaussian assumption and sensitivity to Σ\SigmaΣ estimation in high dimension (shrinkage helps).

pythonood_scores.py
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F


def msp_score(logits):
    """Max softmax probability; high = in-distribution."""
    return F.softmax(logits, dim=1).max(dim=1).values


def energy_score(logits, T=1.0):
    """T * logsumexp(z / T); high = in-distribution (negative energy)."""
    return T * torch.logsumexp(logits / T, dim=1)


@torch.no_grad()
def fit_class_gaussians(feats, labels, num_classes):
    """Class means and a SHARED (tied) covariance from penultimate features (N, D)."""
    D = feats.shape[1]
    mus = torch.stack([feats[labels == c].mean(0) for c in range(num_classes)])  # (K, D)
    centered = feats - mus[labels]
    cov = centered.T @ centered / feats.shape[0]
    cov += 1e-4 * torch.eye(D, device=feats.device)                              # shrinkage for stability
    return mus, torch.linalg.inv(cov)


def mahalanobis_score(feats, mus, prec):
    """Negative minimum squared Mahalanobis distance to any class mean."""
    diff = feats[:, None, :] - mus[None, :, :]                  # (N, K, D)
    d2 = torch.einsum("nkd,de,nke->nk", diff, prec, diff)       # (N, K)
    return -d2.min(dim=1).values


def auroc(score_id, score_ood):
    """Probability that a random ID sample scores higher than a random OOD sample (rank statistic)."""
    s = torch.cat([score_id, score_ood])
    labels = torch.cat([torch.ones_like(score_id), torch.zeros_like(score_ood)])
    order = s.argsort()
    ranks = torch.empty_like(order, dtype=torch.float)
    ranks[order] = torch.arange(1, len(s) + 1, dtype=torch.float)
    n1, n0 = len(score_id), len(score_ood)
    return ((ranks[labels == 1].sum() - n1 * (n1 + 1) / 2) / (n1 * n0)).item()
What OOD detection cannot do

No detector is universally good. Without access to OOD data there is a fundamental ambiguity about what "different" means, and results are very dependent on the ID/OOD pair. Evaluations that tune the detector's hyperparameters on the test OOD set overstate performance. Detectors trained with outlier exposure (Hendrycks, Mazeika and Dietterich, 2019: train the classifier to output a uniform distribution on a large auxiliary set of outliers) generalize well to unseen OOD data in practice, but they are not guaranteed to.

Uncertainty estimation

Aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty

A softmax output is a number between zero and one, but it hides two very different kinds of "I don't know".

  • Aleatoric uncertainty (from Latin alea, dice) is irreducible noise in the data-generating process: two identical-looking X-rays with different diagnoses, a blurry digit between a 4 and a 9, sensor noise. More data does not reduce it; it only lets you estimate it better. It can depend on the input (heteroscedastic): a self-driving system should be less sure at night than at noon.
  • Epistemic uncertainty (from episteme, knowledge) is uncertainty about the model: many functions fit the finite training set and they disagree away from it. More data in the right places reduces it. This is the uncertainty that matters for OOD inputs, active learning and exploration.

Bayesian reasoning draws the line cleanly. With a posterior p(θ∣D)p(\boldsymbol{\theta}\mid\mathcal{D})p(θ∣D) over parameters, the predictive distribution is p(y∣x,D)=∫p(y∣x,θ) p(θ∣D) dθ  ≈  1M∑m=1Mp(y∣x,θm),θm∼p(θ∣D).p(y\mid\boldsymbol{x},\mathcal{D})=\int p(y\mid\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{\theta})\,p(\boldsymbol{\theta}\mid\mathcal{D})\,d\boldsymbol{\theta}\;\approx\;\frac1M\sum_{m=1}^M p(y\mid\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{\theta}_m),\quad\boldsymbol{\theta}_m\sim p(\boldsymbol{\theta}\mid\mathcal{D}).p(y∣x,D)=∫p(y∣x,θ)p(θ∣D)dθ≈M1​m=1∑M​p(y∣x,θm​),θm​∼p(θ∣D). For classification, the total predictive entropy decomposes (using the mutual information between yyy and θ\boldsymbol{\theta}θ): H[pˉ(y∣x)]⏟total=Eθ H[p(y∣x,θ)]⏟aleatoric (expected entropy)+I[y;θ∣x,D]⏟epistemic (disagreement),\underbrace{\mathcal{H}\big[\bar p(y\mid\boldsymbol{x})\big]}_{\text{total}}=\underbrace{\E_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\,\mathcal{H}\big[p(y\mid\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{\theta})\big]}_{\text{aleatoric (expected entropy)}}+\underbrace{\mathcal{I}\big[y;\boldsymbol{\theta}\mid\boldsymbol{x},\mathcal{D}\big]}_{\text{epistemic (disagreement)}},totalH[pˉ​(y∣x)]​​=aleatoric (expected entropy)Eθ​H[p(y∣x,θ)]​​+epistemic (disagreement)I[y;θ∣x,D]​​, where pˉ=Eθ p(y∣x,θ)\bar p=\E_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\,p(y\mid\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{\theta})pˉ​=Eθ​p(y∣x,θ). If every ensemble member says "50-50", the epistemic term is zero and the aleatoric term is log⁡2\log 2log2. If half say "100% A" and half say "100% B", each member has zero entropy (aleatoric zero), the mean is 50-50, and the whole entropy is epistemic. The decomposition is the main reason ensembles are used for uncertainty rather than a single softmax.

For regression one can use a network that outputs both a mean and a variance, trained with the Gaussian negative log-likelihood L=12log⁡σ2(x)+(y−μ(x))22σ2(x)\mathcal{L}=\tfrac12\log\sigma^2(\boldsymbol{x})+\tfrac{(y-\mu(\boldsymbol{x}))^2}{2\sigma^2(\boldsymbol{x})}L=21​logσ2(x)+2σ2(x)(y−μ(x))2​. The learned σ2(x)\sigma^2(\boldsymbol{x})σ2(x) is aleatoric. (Kendall and Gal, 2017, discuss combining both kinds in vision.) Practical caution: jointly learning μ\muμ and σ\sigmaσ can ignore hard examples by inflating σ\sigmaσ; a warm-up phase or β\betaβ-NLL (Seitzer et al., 2022) mitigates this.

Deep ensembles

Lakshminarayanan, Pritzel and Blundell (NeurIPS 2017) proposed the strikingly simple recipe: train MMM networks (typically 5) from different random initializations (and shuffled data order), then average the predicted probabilities. No Bayesian machinery is needed. Ensembles improve accuracy, calibration and OOD detection together. Why do they work well? Fort, Hu and Lakshminarayanan (2019) argued that independent runs from different initializations land in different modes of the loss landscape (functions that are far apart in function space), whereas samples from a local Bayesian approximation stay within a single mode. Averaging across modes captures more of the posterior's diversity. The cost is MMM times the training and inference compute and memory; cheaper variants include snapshot ensembles, SWAG, BatchEnsemble and distillation of an ensemble into one model.

MC dropout

Gal and Ghahramani (ICML 2016) showed that a network with dropout before weight layers, trained with standard dropout, can be interpreted as an approximate variational Bayesian model. At test time you keep dropout on and average TTT stochastic forward passes:

pˉ(y∣x)≈1T∑t=1Tsoftmax⁡(fθ⊙mt(x)),mt∼Bernoulli(1−p).\bar p(y\mid\boldsymbol{x})\approx\frac1T\sum_{t=1}^T\softmax\big(f_{\boldsymbol{\theta}\odot\boldsymbol{m}_t}(\boldsymbol{x})\big),\qquad \boldsymbol{m}_t\sim\text{Bernoulli}(1-p).pˉ​(y∣x)≈T1​t=1∑T​softmax(fθ⊙mt​​(x)),mt​∼Bernoulli(1−p).

It is almost free to adopt (no retraining) and decent for detecting inputs far from the data, but the approximation is crude: the posterior it represents is a restricted family tied to the dropout rate, and it is typically less diverse than a deep ensemble. Treat it as a cheap baseline.

pythonuncertainty.py
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F


def enable_mc_dropout(model):
    """Put the model in eval mode, but keep dropout layers stochastic."""
    model.eval()
    for m in model.modules():
        if isinstance(m, (nn.Dropout, nn.Dropout2d)):
            m.train()


@torch.no_grad()
def predictive_distribution(models_or_passes):
    """Stack a list of (B, K) probability tensors into (M, B, K) and summarize."""
    P = torch.stack(models_or_passes)                       # (M, B, K)
    mean = P.mean(0)                                        # (B, K) predictive distribution
    eps = 1e-12
    total = -(mean * (mean + eps).log()).sum(-1)            # entropy of the mean
    aleatoric = -(P * (P + eps).log()).sum(-1).mean(0)      # expected entropy
    epistemic = total - aleatoric                           # mutual information (>= 0)
    return mean, total, aleatoric, epistemic


@torch.no_grad()
def mc_dropout_predict(model, x, T=30):
    enable_mc_dropout(model)
    passes = [F.softmax(model(x), dim=1) for _ in range(T)]
    return predictive_distribution(passes)


@torch.no_grad()
def ensemble_predict(models, x):
    passes = []
    for m in models:
        m.eval()
        passes.append(F.softmax(m(x), dim=1))
    return predictive_distribution(passes)

Calibration

A classifier is calibrated if its confidence matches its accuracy: among all predictions made with confidence 0.8, 80% should be correct. Formally, with prediction y^\hat yy^​ and confidence p^=max⁡cpc\hat p=\max_c p_cp^​=maxc​pc​, perfect calibration means P(y^=y∣p^=p)=p\P(\hat y=y\mid\hat p=p)=pP(y^​=y∣p^​=p)=p for all p∈[0,1]p\in[0,1]p∈[0,1]. Calibration matters whenever the probability is used: to decide whether to defer to a human, to combine with costs, to feed into another model.

Guo, Pleiss, Sun and Weinberger (ICML 2017) made a point that surprised many: modern deep networks (ResNets, DenseNets) are much more overconfident than the shallower LeNet-era networks, even though they are more accurate. They traced the effect to model capacity, batch normalization, weight decay and, above all, training to near-zero cross-entropy: once the training set is separated the loss can only go down by inflating logit norms.

Reliability diagram. Bin test predictions by confidence into BBB bins I1,…,IBI_1,\dots,I_BI1​,…,IB​ (equal width, e.g. 10 bins). For each bin bbb compute accuracy acc(b)=1∣Ib∣∑i∈Ib1[y^i=yi]\mathrm{acc}(b)=\frac1{\abs{I_b}}\sum_{i\in I_b}\ind[\hat y_i=y_i]acc(b)=∣Ib​∣1​∑i∈Ib​​1[y^​i​=yi​] and mean confidence conf(b)\mathrm{conf}(b)conf(b). Plot accuracy against confidence; the diagonal is perfect calibration; bars below the diagonal indicate overconfidence.

Expected Calibration Error (ECE) summarizes the diagram: ECE=∑b=1B∣Ib∣n ∣acc(b)−conf(b)∣.\mathrm{ECE}=\sum_{b=1}^B\frac{\abs{I_b}}{n}\,\big|\mathrm{acc}(b)-\mathrm{conf}(b)\big|.ECE=b=1∑B​n∣Ib​∣​​acc(b)−conf(b)​. ECE is a weighted gap between the bars and the diagonal. It has caveats: it depends on the number and placement of bins (use equal-mass bins or more samples to reduce bias), it only looks at the top-label confidence, and a classifier that always predicts the base rates can have ECE near zero while being useless. Report it together with accuracy, NLL and the Brier score. Proper scoring rules (NLL, Brier) reward calibration and sharpness (confident correct predictions), whereas ECE rewards calibration alone.

pythoncalibration.py
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F


def reliability_bins(probs, labels, n_bins=10):
    """Return per-bin (count, mean confidence, accuracy) and ECE for top-label confidence."""
    conf, pred = probs.max(dim=1)
    correct = (pred == labels).float()
    edges = torch.linspace(0, 1, n_bins + 1)
    ece, rows = 0.0, []
    for lo, hi in zip(edges[:-1], edges[1:]):
        m = (conf > lo) & (conf <= hi)
        if m.any():
            acc_b, conf_b = correct[m].mean().item(), conf[m].mean().item()
            ece += m.float().mean().item() * abs(acc_b - conf_b)
            rows.append((int(m.sum()), conf_b, acc_b))
        else:
            rows.append((0, float("nan"), float("nan")))
    return rows, ece


def fit_temperature(logits, labels, steps=200, lr=0.05):
    """Learn a scalar T > 0 minimizing NLL of softmax(logits / T) on a held-out set."""
    log_t = torch.zeros(1, requires_grad=True)       # T = exp(log_t) keeps T positive
    opt = torch.optim.Adam([log_t], lr=lr)
    for _ in range(steps):
        opt.zero_grad()
        loss = F.cross_entropy(logits / log_t.exp(), labels)
        loss.backward()
        opt.step()
    return log_t.exp().item()

Temperature scaling. The simplest post-hoc fix (Guo et al.): divide all logits by a single scalar T>0T>0T>0 learned on a held-out validation set by minimizing NLL, p^=softmax⁡(z/T)\hat p=\softmax(\boldsymbol{z}/T)p^​=softmax(z/T). Because dividing all logits by the same positive number never changes their order, the predicted class and accuracy are unchanged; only the confidence moves. T>1T>1T>1 softens (reduces overconfidence), T<1T<1T<1 sharpens. The NLL is convex in 1/T1/T1/T (it is a log-sum-exp minus a linear term), so the fit is a one-dimensional convex problem and works with only a few hundred validation examples. More flexible variants (vector scaling, matrix scaling, Dirichlet calibration) need more data and often overfit. Temperature scaling fixes only marginal miscalibration; it does not help with distribution shift (calibration degrades there, Ovadia et al. 2019, where deep ensembles were the strongest method among those compared).

To make this concrete, I simulated a 10-class classifier whose logits are 2.5 times too large (a perfectly calibrated logit vector multiplied by 2.5), on 5000 samples. It is 52% accurate and its ECE is 0.254; temperature scaling with T=2.5T=2.5T=2.5 brings the ECE to 0.014 without changing a single prediction.

Conformal prediction

Calibration says "when I say 80%, I am right 80% of the time on average". It does not say anything about this input, and requires trusting the model. Conformal prediction (Vovk, Gammerman and Shafer; modern introduction by Angelopoulos and Bates, 2021) wraps any model in a procedure that outputs a set of labels C(x)\mathcal{C}(\boldsymbol{x})C(x) with a finite-sample, distribution-free guarantee, assuming only that calibration and test points are exchangeable (e.g. i.i.d. from the same distribution).

Split conformal recipe for target miscoverage α\alphaα (say 0.10.10.1 for 90% coverage):

  1. Hold out a calibration set {(xi,yi)}i=1n\{(\boldsymbol{x}_i,y_i)\}_{i=1}^n{(xi​,yi​)}i=1n​ unused in training.
  2. Define a nonconformity score s(x,y)s(\boldsymbol{x},y)s(x,y), larger meaning "this label looks worse for this input". A common choice is s(x,y)=1−py(x)s(\boldsymbol{x},y)=1-p_y(\boldsymbol{x})s(x,y)=1−py​(x), one minus the softmax probability of the true label.
  3. Compute scores si=s(xi,yi)s_i=s(\boldsymbol{x}_i,y_i)si​=s(xi​,yi​) on the calibration set and let q^\hat qq^​ be the ⌈(n+1)(1−α)⌉/n\lceil(n+1)(1-\alpha)\rceil/n⌈(n+1)(1−α)⌉/n empirical quantile of s1,…,sns_1,\dots,s_ns1​,…,sn​.
  4. For a new input, output C(xnew)={y: s(xnew,y)≤q^}\mathcal{C}(\boldsymbol{x}_{\text{new}})=\{y:\ s(\boldsymbol{x}_{\text{new}},y)\le\hat q\}C(xnew​)={y: s(xnew​,y)≤q^​}.
Why the coverage guarantee holds

Let sn+1=s(xn+1,yn+1)s_{n+1}=s(\boldsymbol{x}_{n+1},y_{n+1})sn+1​=s(xn+1​,yn+1​) be the score of the (unseen) test point with its true label. The event "yn+1∈C(xn+1)y_{n+1}\in\mathcal{C}(\boldsymbol{x}_{n+1})yn+1​∈C(xn+1​)" is exactly "sn+1≤q^s_{n+1}\le\hat qsn+1​≤q^​". Since the n+1n+1n+1 scores s1,…,sn+1s_1,\dots,s_{n+1}s1​,…,sn+1​ are exchangeable, the rank of sn+1s_{n+1}sn+1​ among them is uniform on {1,…,n+1}\{1,\dots,n+1\}{1,…,n+1} (ignoring ties). The event sn+1≤q^s_{n+1}\le\hat qsn+1​≤q^​, where q^\hat qq^​ is the kkk-th smallest calibration score with k=⌈(n+1)(1−α)⌉k=\lceil(n+1)(1-\alpha)\rceilk=⌈(n+1)(1−α)⌉, occurs iff the test score's rank is at most kkk, which has probability k/(n+1)≥1−αk/(n+1)\ge 1-\alphak/(n+1)≥1−α. So 1−α ≤ P(yn+1∈C(xn+1)) ≤ 1−α+1n+1.1-\alpha\ \le\ \P\big(y_{n+1}\in\mathcal{C}(\boldsymbol{x}_{n+1})\big)\ \le\ 1-\alpha+\frac1{n+1}.1−α ≤ P(yn+1​∈C(xn+1​)) ≤ 1−α+n+11​. The upper bound holds when scores are almost surely distinct. This is a marginal guarantee: it averages over the calibration draw and the test point. It does not promise 90%90\%90% coverage for each class, subgroup or individual input (conditional coverage is impossible to guarantee distribution-free), and it breaks under distribution shift because exchangeability fails.

The size of the set carries the uncertainty: a confident model yields singletons, a confused one returns several labels, and a hopeless input returns many. Better models yield smaller sets at the same coverage. Adaptive scores (APS, Romano et al. 2020; RAPS, Angelopoulos et al. 2021) give sets whose size tracks difficulty better than 1−py1-p_y1−py​. For regression, conformalized quantile regression (Romano, Patterson and Candes, 2019) gives intervals with adaptive width.

pythonconformal.py
import numpy as np


def split_conformal_threshold(cal_probs, cal_labels, alpha=0.1):
    """cal_probs: (n, K) softmax outputs on a held-out calibration set; returns the quantile q_hat."""
    n = len(cal_labels)
    scores = 1.0 - cal_probs[np.arange(n), cal_labels]          # nonconformity of the true label
    k = int(np.ceil((n + 1) * (1 - alpha)))                      # finite-sample corrected rank
    k = min(k, n)
    return np.sort(scores)[k - 1]


def prediction_sets(probs, q_hat):
    """Boolean mask (m, K): label j is in the set iff 1 - p_j <= q_hat."""
    return (1.0 - probs) <= q_hat


def evaluate(sets, labels):
    covered = sets[np.arange(len(labels)), labels].mean()
    avg_size = sets.sum(1).mean()
    return covered, avg_size

Interpretability and explainability

What we want from an explanation

An explanation should help a person do something: debug a model, decide whether to trust a prediction, discover a spurious cue, satisfy a regulator, or learn something about the world. Keep two properties apart. Faithfulness asks whether the explanation reflects what the model actually computes. Plausibility asks whether it looks reasonable to a human. They are different, and visually pleasing maps can be unfaithful. Adebayo et al. (NeurIPS 2018, "Sanity checks for saliency maps") showed that several popular methods produce nearly the same map when the network's weights are randomized, meaning the map reflected image edges more than the model. Always run such sanity checks: randomize the weights (a faithful explanation must change), and measure deletion and insertion curves (remove the most important pixels first; a faithful map makes the confidence fall fast).

Gradient saliency and its relatives

The simplest attribution is the gradient of the class score with respect to the input, Sc(x)=∂zc/∂xS_c(\boldsymbol{x})=\partial z_c/\partial\boldsymbol{x}Sc​(x)=∂zc​/∂x (Simonyan, Vedaldi and Zisserman, 2014, whose saliency map is the per-pixel maximum of the absolute value over colour channels). By the first-order Taylor expansion zc(x+δ)≈zc(x)+Sc⊤δz_c(\boldsymbol{x}+\boldsymbol{\delta})\approx z_c(\boldsymbol{x})+S_c^\top\boldsymbol{\delta}zc​(x+δ)≈zc​(x)+Sc⊤​δ, it measures local sensitivity: how much a small change at each pixel changes the score. This is the same quantity that FGSM uses, and the maps look just as noisy for the same reason: the gradient of a ReLU network fluctuates rapidly (it is piecewise constant), so neighbouring pixels can have unrelated gradients.

Related variants: Gradient times input (x⊙∂zc/∂x\boldsymbol{x}\odot\partial z_c/\partial\boldsymbol{x}x⊙∂zc​/∂x), guided backpropagation (Springenberg et al. 2015, which zeroes negative gradients at ReLUs and is notorious for acting like an edge detector independent of the weights) and DeconvNet. The first-order view is also a limitation: gradients are local, so saturated units give zero gradient even when the feature is decisive.

SmoothGrad

Smilkov et al. (2017) reduce the noise by averaging gradients of noisy copies of the input: S^c(x)=1N∑n=1N∂zc∂x∣x+ηn,ηn∼N(0,σ2I).\hat S_c(\boldsymbol{x})=\frac1N\sum_{n=1}^N\frac{\partial z_c}{\partial\boldsymbol{x}}\Big|_{\boldsymbol{x}+\boldsymbol{\eta}_n},\qquad\boldsymbol{\eta}_n\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2 I).S^c​(x)=N1​n=1∑N​∂x∂zc​​​x+ηn​​,ηn​∼N(0,σ2I). This is the gradient of the Gaussian-smoothed score Eη[zc(x+η)]\E_{\boldsymbol{\eta}}[z_c(\boldsymbol{x}+\boldsymbol{\eta})]Eη​[zc​(x+η)], which removes the high-frequency fluctuations. The noise scale σ\sigmaσ is typically 10-20% of the input range and NNN about 50. Smoothing is the same trick that underlies randomized smoothing for certified defenses, applied to a different goal. It improves visual quality; whether it improves faithfulness depends on the test used.

Grad-CAM

Saliency maps are pixel-level and noisy. CNNs, though, build up spatial feature maps in their last convolutional layer, with each channel acting like a detector for some pattern, and the class decision is a function of those channels. Grad-CAM (Selvaraju et al., ICCV 2017) produces a coarse localization map for class ccc from that layer. Let Ak∈RH×WA^k\in\R^{H\times W}Ak∈RH×W be the activation of channel kkk (there are KKK channels) in the chosen convolutional layer, and ycy^cyc the pre-softmax score of class ccc.

Derivation of Grad-CAM from a global-average-pooling network

Start with the simplest architecture that supports a class activation map (CAM, Zhou et al. 2016): the last conv layer is followed by global average pooling and a linear layer, yc=∑kwkc Fk,Fk=1Z∑i,jAijk,Z=HW.y^c=\sum_k w^c_k\,F^k,\qquad F^k=\frac1{Z}\sum_{i,j}A^k_{ij},\quad Z=HW.yc=k∑​wkc​Fk,Fk=Z1​i,j∑​Aijk​,Z=HW. Substituting, yc=∑i,j1Z∑kwkcAijky^c=\sum_{i,j}\frac1Z\sum_k w^c_kA^k_{ij}yc=∑i,j​Z1​∑k​wkc​Aijk​. So ycy^cyc is a sum over spatial positions of Lijc=1Z∑kwkcAijkL^c_{ij}=\frac1Z\sum_kw^c_kA^k_{ij}Lijc​=Z1​∑k​wkc​Aijk​, and the class activation map ∑kwkcAijk\sum_kw^c_kA^k_{ij}∑k​wkc​Aijk​ tells how much each position contributes. Now compute the gradient of ycy^cyc with respect to the activation AijkA^k_{ij}Aijk​: since AijkA^k_{ij}Aijk​ appears only in FkF^kFk, ∂yc∂Aijk=∂yc∂Fk⋅∂Fk∂Aijk=wkc⋅1Z\frac{\partial y^c}{\partial A^k_{ij}}=\frac{\partial y^c}{\partial F^k}\cdot\frac{\partial F^k}{\partial A^k_{ij}}=w^c_k\cdot\frac1Z∂Aijk​∂yc​=∂Fk∂yc​⋅∂Aijk​∂Fk​=wkc​⋅Z1​. Summing over positions gives ∑i,j∂yc∂Aijk=Z⋅wkcZ=wkc\sum_{i,j}\frac{\partial y^c}{\partial A^k_{ij}}=Z\cdot\frac{w^c_k}{Z}=w^c_k∑i,j​∂Aijk​∂yc​=Z⋅Zwkc​​=wkc​, so the weight of channel kkk equals the globally averaged gradient up to the constant ZZZ: αkc=1Z∑i,j∂yc∂Aijk  ⟹  αkc∝wkc.\alpha^c_k=\frac1Z\sum_{i,j}\frac{\partial y^c}{\partial A^k_{ij}}\ \ \Longrightarrow\ \ \alpha^c_k\propto w^c_k.αkc​=Z1​i,j∑​∂Aijk​∂yc​  ⟹  αkc​∝wkc​. This identity is the key: in a GAP network, the CAM channel weights are the pooled gradients. Grad-CAM defines the weights by that formula for any differentiable network (with a conv layer, followed by arbitrary layers, e.g. fully connected heads, or captioning models), giving   LGrad-CAMc=ReLU⁡(∑kαkcAk),αkc=1Z∑i,j∂yc∂Aijk  \boxed{\;L^c_{\text{Grad-CAM}}=\relu\Big(\sum_k\alpha^c_k A^k\Big),\qquad\alpha^c_k=\frac1Z\sum_{i,j}\frac{\partial y^c}{\partial A^k_{ij}}\;}LGrad-CAMc​=ReLU(k∑​αkc​Ak),αkc​=Z1​i,j∑​∂Aijk​∂yc​​ The ReLU keeps only features with a positive influence on class ccc (negative regions likely belong to other classes). The map has the resolution of the conv layer (7×77\times77×7 for ResNet-50's last block on a 224×224224\times224224×224 image) and is upsampled bilinearly to the image size for display.

Practicalities. Choose the last conv layer (deeper means more semantic, coarser; shallower means finer, less class-specific). Use the logit, not the softmax probability: the softmax gradient of a class is dominated by competition with other classes and can vanish when the class is already confident. Guided Grad-CAM multiplies the upsampled map by guided backpropagation for a high-resolution, class-discriminative picture, but inherits guided backprop's weight-insensitivity problem. Grad-CAM++ (Chattopadhay et al., 2018) uses higher-order terms to better handle multiple instances of a class.

pythongradcam.py
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F
import torchvision


class GradCAM:
    """Grad-CAM for any CNN. `layer` is the nn.Module whose output (B, K, H, W) is explained."""

    def __init__(self, model, layer):
        self.model, self.acts = model.eval(), None
        layer.register_forward_hook(self._save_activation)

    def _save_activation(self, module, inp, out):
        self.acts = out
        out.retain_grad()                      # we want d y^c / d A for this non-leaf tensor

    def __call__(self, x, class_idx=None):
        logits = self.model(x)                 # (B, num_classes), pre-softmax scores
        if class_idx is None:
            class_idx = logits.argmax(1)       # explain the predicted class
        score = logits.gather(1, class_idx.view(-1, 1)).sum()
        self.model.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)
        score.backward()
        A, G = self.acts.detach(), self.acts.grad          # both (B, K, H, W)
        alpha = G.mean(dim=(2, 3), keepdim=True)           # (B, K, 1, 1): global-average-pooled gradients
        cam = F.relu((alpha * A).sum(dim=1, keepdim=True)) # (B, 1, H, W)
        cam = F.interpolate(cam, size=x.shape[-2:], mode="bilinear", align_corners=False)
        cam = cam - cam.amin(dim=(2, 3), keepdim=True)
        cam = cam / (cam.amax(dim=(2, 3), keepdim=True) + 1e-8)   # normalize to [0, 1] per image
        return cam.squeeze(1), class_idx


if __name__ == "__main__":
    model = torchvision.models.resnet18(weights="IMAGENET1K_V1")
    cam_fn = GradCAM(model, model.layer4)       # last residual stage, output (B, 512, 7, 7)
    x = torch.randn(2, 3, 224, 224)             # replace by real, normalized images
    cam, cls = cam_fn(x)
    print(cam.shape, cls)                        # torch.Size([2, 224, 224])

Integrated Gradients

Plain gradients have a famous failure: saturation. If a feature pushes the logit to a plateau, the gradient there is zero even though the feature caused the output. Sundararajan, Taly and Yan (ICML 2017) proposed to accumulate gradients along a path from a baseline x′\boldsymbol{x}'x′ (a "no information" input such as a black image or zeros) to the input x\boldsymbol{x}x:

IGi(x)=(xi−xi′)∫01∂F(x′+t(x−x′))∂xi dt,\mathrm{IG}_i(\boldsymbol{x})=(x_i-x'_i)\int_0^1\frac{\partial F\big(\boldsymbol{x}'+t(\boldsymbol{x}-\boldsymbol{x}')\big)}{\partial x_i}\,dt,IGi​(x)=(xi​−xi′​)∫01​∂xi​∂F(x′+t(x−x′))​dt,

where FFF is the scalar output being explained (e.g. the class logit or probability). In practice, a Riemann sum with mmm steps (20 to 300) approximates the integral.

Axioms. The paper derives IG as the unique (up to path choice) method satisfying two desiderata, and it also satisfies several more.

  • Completeness (sensitivity-a): attributions sum to the difference in output between input and baseline, ∑iIGi(x)=F(x)−F(x′)\sum_i\mathrm{IG}_i(\boldsymbol{x})=F(\boldsymbol{x})-F(\boldsymbol{x}')∑i​IGi​(x)=F(x)−F(x′). Proof: by the fundamental theorem of calculus applied to g(t)=F(x′+t(x−x′))g(t)=F(\boldsymbol{x}'+t(\boldsymbol{x}-\boldsymbol{x}'))g(t)=F(x′+t(x−x′)), F(x)−F(x′)=∫01g′(t)dt=∫01∑i∂F∂xi(xi−xi′) dt=∑iIGiF(\boldsymbol{x})-F(\boldsymbol{x}')=\int_0^1g'(t)dt=\int_0^1\sum_i\frac{\partial F}{\partial x_i}(x_i-x'_i)\,dt=\sum_i\mathrm{IG}_iF(x)−F(x′)=∫01​g′(t)dt=∫01​∑i​∂xi​∂F​(xi​−xi′​)dt=∑i​IGi​. In code this is a free correctness check: if the sum is far from F(x)−F(x′)F(\boldsymbol{x})-F(\boldsymbol{x}')F(x)−F(x′), increase the number of steps.
  • Sensitivity (b): if FFF depends on feature iii and the input and baseline differ only in feature iii with different outputs, then IGi≠0\mathrm{IG}_i\ne0IGi​=0. Plain gradients violate this under saturation.
  • Implementation invariance: two functionally equivalent networks get identical attributions, because IG depends only on gradients of the function, not the architecture. (Methods that propagate custom backward rules, such as DeepLIFT variants and LRP, can violate it.)
  • Linearity and symmetry-preservation: attributions of a weighted sum of models are the weighted sum of attributions, and symmetric features get equal attributions.
The baseline is a modelling decision

The baseline defines what "absence" means, and attributions are always relative to it. A black baseline gives zero attribution to black pixels in the input regardless of their role. Alternatives are a blurred image, noise, the dataset mean, or averaging over several baselines (expected gradients, Erion et al. 2021). Never present an IG map without naming the baseline.

pythonintegrated_gradients.py
import torch


def integrated_gradients(model, x, target, baseline=None, steps=64):
    """x: (B, C, H, W); target: (B,) class indices. Returns attributions with the shape of x."""
    model.eval()
    if baseline is None:
        baseline = torch.zeros_like(x)
    # midpoint Riemann sum over alpha in (0, 1): shape (steps,) -> broadcast over the batch
    alphas = (torch.arange(steps, dtype=x.dtype, device=x.device) + 0.5) / steps
    total = torch.zeros_like(x)
    for a in alphas:
        xi = (baseline + a * (x - baseline)).requires_grad_(True)
        out = model(xi).gather(1, target.view(-1, 1)).sum()   # use the logit of the target class
        grad, = torch.autograd.grad(out, xi)
        total += grad
    attr = (x - baseline) * total / steps
    # completeness check: sum of attributions should be close to F(x) - F(baseline)
    with torch.no_grad():
        delta = (model(x).gather(1, target.view(-1, 1)) - model(baseline).gather(1, target.view(-1, 1))).squeeze(1)
    gap = (attr.flatten(1).sum(1) - delta).abs().max().item()
    print(f"max completeness error: {gap:.4f}  (increase `steps` if large)")
    return attr


def smoothgrad(model, x, target, n=50, sigma=0.15):
    """Average input-gradients over n noisy copies; sigma is a fraction of the input range."""
    model.eval()
    span = (x.max() - x.min()).item()
    total = torch.zeros_like(x)
    for _ in range(n):
        xn = (x + sigma * span * torch.randn_like(x)).requires_grad_(True)
        out = model(xn).gather(1, target.view(-1, 1)).sum()
        grad, = torch.autograd.grad(out, xn)
        total += grad
    return total / n

Attention analysis and its caveats

Transformers expose attention weights softmax(QK⊤/dk)\mathrm{softmax}(QK^\top/\sqrt{d_k})softmax(QK⊤/dk​​) that look like a ready-made explanation: "the model looked at these words". Jain and Wallace (2019, "Attention is not explanation") found that attention weights often correlate poorly with gradient-based importance and that very different attention distributions can give the same prediction; Wiegreffe and Pinter (2019, "Attention is not not explanation") replied that the answer depends on what claim you make and what you test. The caveats worth remembering:

  • The attention output is a weighted sum of value vectors, which are then mixed by output projections, residual connections, MLPs and later layers. A large weight on a token with a small-norm value contributes little (Kobayashi et al. 2020 proposed norm-based analysis).
  • Information is mixed across layers: by layer 6 the representation at position iii contains information from many positions, so raw attention in higher layers does not say where information came from. Attention rollout and attention flow (Abnar and Zuidema, 2020) multiply attention matrices across layers (with the residual identity added) to approximate the flow; they are heuristics.
  • Multiple heads do different things, and many can be pruned (Michel et al. 2019; Voita et al. 2019), so a head's pattern is not necessarily important.
  • Attention is a mechanism, not an attribution. Use it as a hypothesis generator, then test it by intervention (ablate or patch a head and see what changes).

Probing and its pitfalls

A probe is a small classifier trained on frozen representations to predict a property (part of speech, syntactic depth, board state in a game, the colour of an object). If a linear probe predicts the property from layer ℓ\ellℓ, the information is linearly decodable there. Alain and Bengio (2017) introduced linear classifier probes; Hewitt and Manning (2019) found structure in BERT's geometry reflecting syntax trees.

The pitfalls are significant and well documented.

  1. Probe capacity. A powerful probe (an MLP) can learn the task itself from the raw input, so high accuracy says nothing about the representation. Hewitt and Liang (2019) proposed control tasks: the same probe on random labels per word type; selectivity is task accuracy minus control accuracy. Use simple (linear) probes, report baselines (probe on random-initialized network, on input embeddings), and compare with the best from-scratch model.
  2. Decodable is not used. The model may encode a feature that the downstream computation ignores. To test use, intervene: edit the representation along the probe direction and see whether the output changes (Elazar et al., 2021, amnesic probing, removes the information and measures the effect; Ravfogel et al.'s INLP iteratively projects out linear directions).
  3. Correlation with confounds. The probe may exploit a correlate (position, frequency, a shortcut) rather than the property.
  4. Mutual-information view. Because accuracy depends on the probe's learning curve, information-theoretic probes (Voita and Titov, 2020, minimum description length) report the code length of the labels given the representations, which accounts for how much data the probe needs.

Mechanistic interpretability (overview)

Mechanistic interpretability aims to reverse-engineer networks into human-understandable algorithms, treating the trained weights as a program to be understood rather than a black box to be summarized by correlations. The programme has a few central ideas.

  • Features and circuits. Olah et al. (Distill, 2020, "Zoom in") argued that networks consist of features (directions in activation space that correspond to meaningful properties, such as curve detectors in vision models) connected by weights into circuits: subgraphs implementing an identifiable computation. In transformers, Elhage et al. (2021, "A mathematical framework for transformer circuits") decomposed the residual stream view, in which each attention head and MLP reads from and writes to a shared stream, and identified induction heads (Olsson et al. 2022): a pair of heads that implements "if token AAA was followed by BBB earlier in the context, and AAA appears again, predict BBB", a mechanism behind in-context copying and linked to the sudden formation of in-context learning during training. Wang et al. (2022) traced a full circuit for indirect-object identification in GPT-2 small.
  • Causal tools. Observing activations is not enough. Activation patching (also causal tracing, used by Meng et al., 2022, to locate factual associations in mid-layer MLPs) copies an activation from one run into another and measures the effect on the output. Ablation removes a component. Logit lens reads the residual stream through the unembedding at each layer. These interventions produce causal claims, unlike saliency.
  • Superposition. If each neuron represented one feature, a network of ddd neurons could represent only ddd features. Real networks seem to represent more features than dimensions by storing them as non-orthogonal directions, relying on features being sparse (rarely active together) so interference is tolerable. Elhage et al. (2022, "Toy models of superposition") showed this in small ReLU networks: with sparse features, the optimal solution packs n>dn>dn>d features into ddd dimensions as geometric arrangements (pentagons in 2D). The consequence is polysemantic neurons: single neurons that respond to several unrelated things, making neuron-by-neuron analysis unreliable.
  • Sparse autoencoders (SAEs). If activations a∈Rd\boldsymbol{a}\in\R^da∈Rd are sparse combinations of n≫dn\gg dn≫d feature directions, learn them as a dictionary: f=ReLU⁡(We(a−bd)+be)∈Rn,a^=Wdf+bd,L=∥a−a^∥22+λ∥f∥1.\boldsymbol{f}=\relu(W_e(\boldsymbol{a}-\boldsymbol{b}_d)+\boldsymbol{b}_e)\in\R^n,\qquad\hat{\boldsymbol{a}}=W_d\boldsymbol{f}+\boldsymbol{b}_d,\qquad\mathcal{L}=\norm{\boldsymbol{a}-\hat{\boldsymbol{a}}}_2^2+\lambda\norm{\boldsymbol{f}}_1.f=ReLU(We​(a−bd​)+be​)∈Rn,a^=Wd​f+bd​,L=∥a−a^∥22​+λ∥f∥1​. The ℓ1\ell_1ℓ1​ penalty encourages few active features per input, and each column of WdW_dWd​ is a candidate feature direction. Bricken et al. (Anthropic, 2023, "Towards monosemanticity") and Cunningham et al. (2023) applied this to small language models and found many interpretable features; later work scaled SAEs to larger models (Templeton et al. 2024, "Scaling monosemanticity"; also top-kkk and gated SAE variants). The picture is encouraging but incomplete: SAEs have reconstruction error that harms the model's loss when spliced in, features can split or merge as the dictionary grows, "dead" features occur, and it remains debated how faithfully features capture the model's own computation.
pythonsparse_autoencoder.py
import torch
import torch.nn as nn


class SparseAutoencoder(nn.Module):
    """Overcomplete dictionary learning on activations a in R^d with n_features >> d."""

    def __init__(self, d, n_features):
        super().__init__()
        self.W_enc = nn.Linear(d, n_features)
        self.W_dec = nn.Linear(n_features, d, bias=False)
        self.b_dec = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(d))
        with torch.no_grad():                       # unit-norm decoder columns
            self.W_dec.weight.copy_(nn.functional.normalize(self.W_dec.weight, dim=0))

    def forward(self, a):
        f = torch.relu(self.W_enc(a - self.b_dec))  # (B, n_features), sparse after training
        a_hat = self.W_dec(f) + self.b_dec          # (B, d)
        return a_hat, f

    @torch.no_grad()
    def renormalize(self):
        """Keep decoder columns at unit norm so the L1 penalty cannot be cheated by shrinking f."""
        self.W_dec.weight.copy_(nn.functional.normalize(self.W_dec.weight, dim=0))


def train_sae(acts, n_features=512, l1=1e-3, epochs=20, bs=256, lr=1e-3):
    sae = SparseAutoencoder(acts.shape[1], n_features)
    opt = torch.optim.Adam(sae.parameters(), lr=lr)
    for ep in range(epochs):
        perm = torch.randperm(len(acts))
        for i in range(0, len(acts), bs):
            a = acts[perm[i:i + bs]]
            a_hat, f = sae(a)
            loss = (a - a_hat).pow(2).sum(-1).mean() + l1 * f.abs().sum(-1).mean()
            opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step(); sae.renormalize()
        l0 = (f > 0).float().sum(-1).mean().item()      # average number of active features
        print(f"epoch {ep}: loss {loss.item():.4f}  L0 {l0:.1f}")
    return sae

Fairness and bias audits

Where bias comes from

A model is not biased in a vacuum; harm arises along the whole pipeline. Historical bias: the world is unequal and data record it. Representation bias: some groups are underrepresented in the data (Buolamwini and Gebru, 2018, "Gender Shades", found that commercial gender classifiers had far higher error on darker-skinned women than on lighter-skinned men). Measurement bias: the label is a flawed proxy (arrests for crime, cost for health need; Obermeyer et al., 2019, showed a healthcare risk algorithm underestimated the needs of Black patients because cost was the target). Aggregation bias: one model for groups with different relationships. Feedback loops: model decisions change the data collected next. Language models inherit stereotypes from text (Bolukbasi et al. 2016 on word embeddings; Caliskan et al. 2017). Removing the protected attribute rarely helps ("fairness through unawareness") because other features are proxies for it.

Group fairness metrics

Let Y∈{0,1}Y\in\{0,1\}Y∈{0,1} be the true outcome, Y^∈{0,1}\hat Y\in\{0,1\}Y^∈{0,1} the decision (e.g. approve), and AAA the protected attribute (group). The three standard group criteria differ in what they condition on.

Criterion Requirement Meaning
Demographic parity (statistical parity) P(Y^=1∣A=a)=P(Y^=1∣A=b)\P(\hat Y=1\mid A=a)=\P(\hat Y=1\mid A=b)P(Y^=1∣A=a)=P(Y^=1∣A=b) Same selection rate in every group
Equalized odds (Hardt, Price and Srebro, 2016) P(Y^=1∣Y=y,A=a)\P(\hat Y=1\mid Y=y,A=a)P(Y^=1∣Y=y,A=a) equal across aaa for y=0y=0y=0 and y=1y=1y=1 Same TPR and FPR in every group
Equal opportunity equal TPR only (y=1y=1y=1) Qualified people are accepted equally often
Predictive parity / calibration within groups P(Y=1∣Y^=1,A=a)\P(Y=1\mid\hat Y=1,A=a)P(Y=1∣Y^=1,A=a) (or P(Y=1∣S=s,A=a)=s\P(Y=1\mid S=s,A=a)=sP(Y=1∣S=s,A=a)=s) equal across groups A score means the same thing in each group

Demographic parity ignores the true outcome, so it can force unqualified acceptances if base rates differ, or be satisfied by a useless classifier. Equalized odds takes the labels as ground truth, which is only reasonable if the labels are not themselves biased. Choose the criterion by thinking about the harm: a false positive in recidivism (wrongly labeled high-risk) and a false negative in medical screening (missed disease) have different costs.

A small audit by hand

A loan model on 1000 applicants per group. Group A: 500 repay, model approves 400 of them and 100 of the 500 who default. Group B: 200 repay, model approves 120 of them and 40 of the 800 who default.

  • Approval rate: A =500/1000=0.50= 500/1000=0.50=500/1000=0.50, B =160/1000=0.16= 160/1000=0.16=160/1000=0.16. Demographic parity difference =0.34=0.34=0.34.
  • TPR: A =400/500=0.80=400/500=0.80=400/500=0.80, B =120/200=0.60=120/200=0.60=120/200=0.60. FPR: A =100/500=0.20=100/500=0.20=100/500=0.20, B =40/800=0.05=40/800=0.05=40/800=0.05. Equalized-odds gaps 0.200.200.20 and 0.150.150.15.
  • Precision (predictive parity): A =400/500=0.80=400/500=0.80=400/500=0.80, B =120/160=0.75=120/160=0.75=120/160=0.75. Group B differs in base rate (20% versus 50%), which is exactly why the criteria disagree.

Impossibility results

One would like all of these at once. Kleinberg, Mullainathan and Raghavan (2017) and Chouldechova (2017) showed that this is mathematically impossible except in degenerate cases. A compact derivation: for group aaa with base rate pa=P(Y=1∣A=a)p_a=\P(Y=1\mid A=a)pa​=P(Y=1∣A=a), positive predictive value PPVa\mathrm{PPV}_aPPVa​, false positive rate FPRa\mathrm{FPR}_aFPRa​ and false negative rate FNRa\mathrm{FNR}_aFNRa​, simple Bayes algebra gives the identity

FPRa=pa1−pa⋅1−PPVaPPVa⋅(1−FNRa).\mathrm{FPR}_a=\frac{p_a}{1-p_a}\cdot\frac{1-\mathrm{PPV}_a}{\mathrm{PPV}_a}\cdot\big(1-\mathrm{FNR}_a\big).FPRa​=1−pa​pa​​⋅PPVa​1−PPVa​​⋅(1−FNRa​).

Proof sketch

Write PPV=TPTP+FP\mathrm{PPV}=\frac{TP}{TP+FP}PPV=TP+FPTP​, so FP=TP 1−PPVPPVFP=TP\,\frac{1-\mathrm{PPV}}{\mathrm{PPV}}FP=TPPPV1−PPV​. Divide both sides by the number of negatives N0=n(1−p)N_0=n(1-p)N0​=n(1−p) and write TP=n p (1−FNR)TP=n\,p\,(1-\mathrm{FNR})TP=np(1−FNR): FPR=FPN0=n p (1−FNR)n(1−p)⋅1−PPVPPV.\mathrm{FPR}=\frac{FP}{N_0}=\frac{n\,p\,(1-\mathrm{FNR})}{n(1-p)}\cdot\frac{1-\mathrm{PPV}}{\mathrm{PPV}}.FPR=N0​FP​=n(1−p)np(1−FNR)​⋅PPV1−PPV​. Now suppose two groups have equal PPV (predictive parity) and equal FNR and FPR (equalized odds). The identity then forces pa1−pa=pb1−pb\frac{p_a}{1-p_a}=\frac{p_b}{1-p_b}1−pa​pa​​=1−pb​pb​​, i.e. equal base rates, unless the classifier is perfect (PPV=1\mathrm{PPV}=1PPV=1 and FNR=0\mathrm{FNR}=0FNR=0, making FPR =0=0=0). When base rates differ and the classifier is imperfect, you must give up at least one criterion.

The practical reading: fairness is not a number that a training recipe can drive to zero. It requires a normative choice about which error to equalize, made with the stakeholders affected, and the existence of the trade-off is not evidence of a flawed model but of a real conflict (this is the core of the COMPAS controversy, ProPublica 2016 versus the vendor's reply). Individual fairness (Dwork et al., 2012: similar individuals receive similar outcomes under a task-appropriate similarity metric) and counterfactual fairness (Kusner et al., 2017: the decision would not change had the protected attribute been different in a causal model) offer alternative notions with their own requirements, namely a metric or a causal graph.

Mitigation

Interventions are classified by where in the pipeline they act.

  • Pre-processing: re-sample or re-weight (Kamiran and Calders), collect more data for under-represented groups (usually the highest-impact fix), repair features, remove proxies, and audit labels.
  • In-processing: add a fairness penalty (e.g. difference in selection rates, or an adversary trying to predict AAA from the representation, Zhang, Lemoine and Mitchell 2018; Edwards and Storkey 2016); Group DRO (Sagawa et al. 2020) minimizes the worst-group loss max⁡gEg[ℓ]\max_g\E_g[\ell]maxg​Eg​[ℓ] and needs strong regularization to avoid overfitting small groups.
  • Post-processing: adjust decisions without retraining; Hardt et al. choose group-specific thresholds (possibly randomized) to equalize TPR and FPR. Legal and ethical constraints may forbid using the attribute at decision time, even when mitigating.

Each mitigation trades accuracy, one fairness criterion or another, and sometimes the other groups' welfare. Report subgroup metrics, intersectional groups (e.g. gender by skin type), and confidence intervals, since small groups give noisy estimates.

pythonfairness_audit.py
import numpy as np


def group_rates(y_true, y_pred, group):
    """Per-group selection rate, TPR, FPR and PPV. Inputs are 1D integer arrays."""
    out = {}
    for g in np.unique(group):
        m = group == g
        yt, yp = y_true[m], y_pred[m]
        tp = ((yp == 1) & (yt == 1)).sum()
        fp = ((yp == 1) & (yt == 0)).sum()
        fn = ((yp == 0) & (yt == 1)).sum()
        tn = ((yp == 0) & (yt == 0)).sum()
        out[g] = dict(
            n=int(m.sum()),
            base_rate=float(yt.mean()),
            selection=float(yp.mean()),
            tpr=tp / max(tp + fn, 1),
            fpr=fp / max(fp + tn, 1),
            ppv=tp / max(tp + fp, 1),
        )
    return out


def gaps(rates):
    """Largest between-group gap for each metric (0 means parity)."""
    keys = ["selection", "tpr", "fpr", "ppv"]
    return {k: max(r[k] for r in rates.values()) - min(r[k] for r in rates.values()) for k in keys}


def threshold_for_equal_tpr(scores, y_true, group, target_tpr=0.8):
    """Post-processing: per-group score threshold that achieves the same TPR in every group."""
    thr = {}
    for g in np.unique(group):
        s = scores[(group == g) & (y_true == 1)]
        thr[g] = np.quantile(s, 1 - target_tpr)     # accept the top `target_tpr` fraction of positives
    return thr


# Reproduces the worked example in the text (group A: 500/500 split, group B: 200/800).
yt = np.r_[np.ones(500), np.zeros(500), np.ones(200), np.zeros(800)].astype(int)
yp = np.r_[np.ones(400), np.zeros(100), np.ones(100), np.zeros(400), np.ones(120), np.zeros(80), np.ones(40), np.zeros(760)].astype(int)
grp = np.r_[np.zeros(1000), np.ones(1000)].astype(int)
r = group_rates(yt, yp, grp)
print(r)
print(gaps(r))

Privacy

What can leak

A trained model is a compressed, lossy summary of its training data, and summaries leak. Three increasingly serious attacks illustrate this.

  • Membership inference (Shokri, Stronati, Song and Shmatikov, 2017): given a record and access to the model, decide whether the record was in the training set. The signal is the generalization gap: models are more confident, with lower loss, on points they trained on. The simplest attack thresholds the loss: predict "member" if L(f(x),y)<τ\mathcal{L}(f(\boldsymbol{x}),y)<\tauL(f(x),y)<τ. Shokri et al. trained shadow models to learn the decision rule; Carlini et al. (2022, LiRA) showed that comparing against per-example reference distributions, evaluated at low false-positive rates, is far more powerful than average-case accuracy suggests. Membership of a single patient in a "cancer clinic" training set is itself sensitive.
  • Model inversion and training-data extraction. Fredrikson et al. (2015) reconstructed faces from a face-recognition model's confidence outputs. Carlini et al. (2021) extracted hundreds of verbatim training sequences from GPT-2 by sampling and filtering, and later work showed larger language models memorize more and that duplicated data is memorized most.
  • Memorization is not always overfitting. Feldman (2020) argued that memorizing rare examples is necessary for optimal generalization on long-tailed data; a model can generalize well on average while memorizing individuals.

Empirically, membership attacks succeed more for small training sets, many epochs, large models and overfit training procedures. Regularization, early stopping and more data reduce, but do not eliminate, risk, and they give no quantitative guarantee. Differential privacy does.

Differential privacy: the definition

Imagine two datasets DDD and D′D'D′ that differ in exactly one person's record (neighbouring datasets). A randomized algorithm M\mathcal{M}M is (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta)(ε,δ)-differentially private (Dwork, McSherry, Nissim and Smith, 2006; the δ\deltaδ relaxation by Dwork et al., 2006) if for every pair of neighbours and every set of outputs SSS,
