P[M(D)∈S] ≤ eε P[M(D′)∈S]+δ.\P\big[\mathcal{M}(D)\in S\big]\ \le\ e^{\varepsilon}\,\P\big[\mathcal{M}(D')\in S\big]+\delta.P[M(D)∈S] ≤ eεP[M(D′)∈S]+δ.

The intuition is that an observer looking at the output cannot tell much about whether any one person's data was included: the output distributions with and without that person are within a factor eεe^\varepsiloneε of each other, except on an event of probability δ\deltaδ. The smaller ε\varepsilonε, the stronger the privacy. The guarantee holds against an adversary with arbitrary side information and is a property of the algorithm, not of one output. Key facts:

  • Post-processing: any computation on the output of a DP algorithm, without access to the data, remains DP with the same parameters.
  • Composition: running kkk mechanisms consumes budget. Basic composition gives (kε,kδ)(k\varepsilon,k\delta)(kε,kδ); advanced composition improves this to roughly ε2kln⁡(1/δ′)+kε(eε−1)\varepsilon\sqrt{2k\ln(1/\delta')}+k\varepsilon(e^\varepsilon-1)ε2kln(1/δ′)​+kε(eε−1); modern accountants (moments accountant, Renyi DP, Gaussian DP, privacy-loss distributions) are tighter and are what libraries use.
  • Interpretation of ε\varepsilonε: a hypothesis-testing view says that ε\varepsilonε bounds how well any test can distinguish DDD from D′D'D′; ε≈1\varepsilon\approx 1ε≈1 is considered strong, 8-10 or more weak-but-still-meaningful, and δ\deltaδ should be much smaller than 1/n1/n1/n (typically 10−510^{-5}10−5 or lower). These are conventions, not laws; and the guarantee is on record-level membership, not on harm in general (it does not stop inference about people who are not in the data).

Gaussian mechanism. To release a function q(D)∈Rdq(D)\in\R^dq(D)∈Rd with ℓ2\ell_2ℓ2​ sensitivity Δ2=max⁡D∼D′∥q(D)−q(D′)∥2\Delta_2=\max_{D\sim D'}\norm{q(D)-q(D')}_2Δ2​=maxD∼D′​∥q(D)−q(D′)∥2​, add noise N(0,σ2I)\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2I)N(0,σ2I). The classical analysis shows it is (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta)(ε,δ)-DP for ε∈(0,1)\varepsilon\in(0,1)ε∈(0,1) when σ≥Δ22ln⁡(1.25/δ)/ε\sigma\ge\Delta_2\sqrt{2\ln(1.25/\delta)}/\varepsilonσ≥Δ2​2ln(1.25/δ)​/ε. The noise is calibrated to how much one person can change the answer, not to how much they actually did. That is why DP needs bounded sensitivity (clipping).

DP-SGD

Abadi et al. (CCS 2016, "Deep learning with differential privacy") made DP practical for deep learning. The recipe changes plain SGD in two places, and each has a reason.

  1. Per-example gradient clipping. Compute the gradient gi\boldsymbol{g}_igi​ for each example, and rescale it to norm at most CCC: gˉi=gi/max⁡(1,∥gi∥2/C)\bar{\boldsymbol{g}}_i=\boldsymbol{g}_i/\max(1,\norm{\boldsymbol{g}_i}_2/C)gˉ​i​=gi​/max(1,∥gi​∥2​/C). Now one example's contribution to the summed gradient has norm at most CCC: the sensitivity is bounded. Without clipping, one outlier could move the update arbitrarily far, and no finite amount of noise would hide it.
  2. Gaussian noise. Sum the clipped gradients over a batch of expected size BBB (sampled by Poisson subsampling: each example is included independently with probability q=B/Nq=B/Nq=B/N), add N(0,σ2C2I)\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2C^2I)N(0,σ2C2I) and divide by BBB: g~=1B(∑i∈batchgˉi+N(0,σ2C2I)),θ←θ−η g~.\tilde{\boldsymbol{g}}=\frac1B\Big(\sum_{i\in\text{batch}}\bar{\boldsymbol{g}}_i+\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2C^2 I)\Big),\qquad\boldsymbol{\theta}\leftarrow\boldsymbol{\theta}-\eta\,\tilde{\boldsymbol{g}}.g~​=B1​(i∈batch∑​gˉ​i​+N(0,σ2C2I)),θ←θ−ηg~​. The privacy cost of TTT steps is computed by an accountant, using amplification by subsampling: since each step touches only a fraction qqq of the data, its privacy loss is smaller than that of a full-batch Gaussian mechanism. Given qqq, σ\sigmaσ, TTT and δ\deltaδ, the accountant returns the total ε\varepsilonε.

What drives the privacy-utility trade-off? The noise added to the average gradient has standard deviation σC/B\sigma C/BσC/B per coordinate, so (i) larger batches reduce the noise relative to the signal (DP-SGD works best with very large batches), (ii) more noise per unit ε\varepsilonε is needed as TTT grows, so training must be short, (iii) clipping introduces bias when CCC is much smaller than typical gradient norms, and (iv) the noise is added in all ppp dimensions, so the total noise norm scales like σCp/B\sigma C\sqrt p/BσCp​/B, hurting large models (though gradients often concentrate in a low-dimensional subspace and fine-tuning small adapters can work well). Practical results: DP training on CIFAR-10 reached accuracies in the 60-70% range at ε≈8\varepsilon\approx 8ε≈8 with careful tuning in early work, and later work with large batches, augmentation multiplicity and pretrained backbones (De et al., 2022, and others) closed much of the gap. DP fine-tuning of a model pretrained on public data is the dominant practical recipe.

InteractiveDifferential privacy: noise, clipping and epsilon
pythondp_sgd_manual.py
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F

torch.manual_seed(0)


def dp_sgd_step(model, loss_fn, xb, yb, lr, clip, sigma):
    """One DP-SGD step using torch.func for per-example gradients.
    (Poisson sampling of the batch is assumed to have happened outside, and the privacy
    accountant is a separate component, e.g. from Opacus.)"""
    from torch.func import functional_call, vmap, grad
    params = {k: v.detach() for k, v in model.named_parameters()}

    def per_example_loss(p, x, y):
        out = functional_call(model, p, (x.unsqueeze(0),))
        return loss_fn(out, y.unsqueeze(0))

    g = vmap(grad(per_example_loss), in_dims=(None, 0, 0))(params, xb, yb)   # dict of (B, *shape)
    norms = torch.sqrt(sum(v.flatten(1).pow(2).sum(1) for v in g.values()))  # (B,) per-example L2 norm
    scale = torch.clamp(clip / (norms + 1e-12), max=1.0)                     # = 1 / max(1, ||g|| / C)
    B = xb.shape[0]
    with torch.no_grad():
        for name, p in model.named_parameters():
            clipped_sum = (g[name] * scale.view(-1, *[1] * (g[name].dim() - 1))).sum(0)
            noise = torch.randn_like(p) * sigma * clip
            p -= lr * (clipped_sum + noise) / B


# A tiny demonstration on random data
model = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(20, 32), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(32, 2))
X, Y = torch.randn(256, 20), torch.randint(0, 2, (256,))
for step in range(5):
    idx = torch.rand(256) < 0.25                       # Poisson subsampling with q = 0.25
    dp_sgd_step(model, F.cross_entropy, X[idx], Y[idx], lr=0.5, clip=1.0, sigma=1.0)
    print(step, F.cross_entropy(model(X), Y).item())

In production use a library: Opacus (PyTorch) wraps a model, optimizer and loader with a PrivacyEngine, computes per-sample gradients efficiently with hooks, and tracks ε\varepsilonε with an RDP or PRV accountant.

pythonopacus_example.py
# pip install opacus  (API of Opacus 1.x)
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
from torch.utils.data import DataLoader, TensorDataset
from opacus import PrivacyEngine

X, Y = torch.randn(2000, 20), torch.randint(0, 2, (2000,))
loader = DataLoader(TensorDataset(X, Y), batch_size=128)
model = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(20, 64), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(64, 2))
opt = torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=0.1)

engine = PrivacyEngine()
model, opt, loader = engine.make_private_with_epsilon(
    module=model, optimizer=opt, data_loader=loader,
    target_epsilon=8.0, target_delta=1e-5, epochs=5, max_grad_norm=1.0)

for epoch in range(5):
    for xb, yb in loader:
        opt.zero_grad()
        nn.functional.cross_entropy(model(xb), yb).backward()
        opt.step()
    print(f"epoch {epoch}: epsilon so far = {engine.get_epsilon(delta=1e-5):.2f}")
What DP does and does not give you

DP bounds the influence of any one record. It does not hide properties of the population (a DP model can still learn that smoking predicts cancer), it does not protect an individual whose data appears many times (group privacy degrades as kεk\varepsilonkε for a group of kkk), it protects only if the implementation is right (clipping, Poisson sampling, accounting, secure noise generation), and it has real accuracy costs, which fall hardest on rare subgroups and tail examples (Bagdasaryan et al., 2019, "Differential privacy has disparate impact on model accuracy"). It interacts with fairness. Related tools: federated learning keeps raw data on-device but gradients still leak without DP or secure aggregation; machine unlearning tries to remove a record's influence after training, and has no general efficient exact solution for deep networks.

Safety, red-teaming and responsible release

Thinking about harm

Safety in this setting covers technical failure modes (the model does something unintended), misuse (a person uses it to cause harm) and structural effects (concentration of power, labour, information ecosystems). A useful frame for any model is to enumerate who is affected, how they could be harmed, how likely and how severe the harm is, and what mitigations exist at each stage: data, training, evaluation, release, monitoring. Distinguish capability (what the model can do) from propensity (what it tends to do) and from deployment context (who can access it, with which guardrails).

Model cards and documentation

Mitchell et al. (FAT* 2019, "Model cards for model reporting") proposed a short standard document that accompanies a model. Gebru et al. (2018/2021, "Datasheets for datasets") did the same for data. A good model card states:

  • Intended use and out-of-scope uses; users and contexts it was evaluated for.
  • Training data (sources, collection, licensing, known gaps) and preprocessing.
  • Evaluation: metrics disaggregated by relevant groups and conditions (not just a global average), with confidence intervals, and the evaluation data.
  • Ethical considerations and risks, known failure modes, and limitations.
  • Environment and compute, version, contact, and update policy.

A card is useful only if it contains numbers a reader could be disappointed by. Treat it as part of the engineering process (written during development), not as post-hoc marketing.

Red-teaming and evaluation

Red-teaming is adversarial testing by people (and increasingly models) whose job is to find failures before users do. It complements benchmarks: benchmarks measure known failure modes on fixed data, red teams search for unknown ones, adaptively. Practices that have emerged:

  • Define threat scenarios first (e.g. generation of harmful instructions, privacy leakage, biased outputs, prompt injection through tool outputs, deception), then probe each with diverse testers, including domain experts and people from affected communities.
  • Combine manual and automated red-teaming: Perez et al. (2022) used a language model to generate test cases for another; gradient-based or search-based attacks produce adversarial suffixes (Zou et al. 2023). Automated methods give coverage, humans give creativity.
  • Record failures in a reproducible, versioned test set, fix, and re-test: a fix that moves the failure elsewhere is common. Measure the attack success rate at a fixed budget, and report the attacker's knowledge and effort.
  • Capability evaluations for dangerous capabilities (cyber-offense, bio-chemical uplift, autonomous replication) are run by specialist teams before deployment, with thresholds that trigger stronger safeguards. This is an active, unsettled area.
  • Safeguard layers: training-time alignment (RLHF and related methods, see Week 10 and Week 15), input and output classifiers, rate limits, monitoring, abuse reporting, and the ability to revoke access (feasible for APIs, impossible for open weights).

Misuse and responsible release

Generative models are dual use: the same image model produces art and non-consensual imagery; the same code model writes tools and malware. The release decision has a spectrum: closed (internal), API access (can monitor, filter, revoke), gated weights (research access) and open weights (maximal scientific and economic benefit, no revocation). There is no universal answer; factors include the marginal risk relative to what is available already ("uplift"), the severity and reversibility of potential harm, whether defenses benefit from openness (security research often does), and the capability level. Release practices that help: staged release, documentation (model card, data statement), watermarking or provenance metadata for synthetic media (C2PA, statistical watermarks for text, with known limits: they can be removed by paraphrasing), usage licenses (such as OpenRAIL, enforceable only where there is a way to enforce), and an incident-response process.

For your projects, a practical checklist: write down the intended use and who could be harmed; evaluate on subgroups and shifted data; measure calibration and set an abstention rule; decide what you log (privacy) and how a user can contest a decision; plan monitoring for drift; and say plainly what the model cannot do.

Governance in brief

Regulation is evolving quickly (for instance the EU AI Act's risk-tiered obligations, sector-specific rules in health and finance, and voluntary frameworks such as the NIST AI Risk Management Framework). You do not need the details to start, but you should expect high-stakes deployments to require documentation, testing for bias and robustness, human oversight and traceability, which is why the tools in this chapter are becoming part of the job.

Deep learning theory highlights

Theory for deep learning is in the odd position that practice runs far ahead of it. What we have is a collection of partial explanations, mostly for simplified models (linear, two-layer, infinite-width), plus empirical phenomena that any complete theory must explain. This section picks the results that every practitioner should know. For each, ask: what is proved, under which assumptions, and what does it not explain?

Generalization of overparameterized models

Classical statistical learning theory bounds the gap between training and test error by the capacity of the hypothesis class: VC dimension, Rademacher complexity, or parameter count. A typical bound has the form R(f)≤R^(f)+O(capacity/n)R(f)\le\hat R(f)+O\big(\sqrt{\mathrm{capacity}/n}\big)R(f)≤R^(f)+O(capacity/n​). A modern network has more parameters than training points, can fit any labelling of the data, and so the bound is vacuous. Yet it generalizes. Something other than raw capacity must govern the outcome: the algorithm (SGD), the data, the architecture.

The randomization experiments. Zhang, Bengio, Hardt, Recht and Vinyals (ICLR 2017, "Understanding deep learning requires rethinking generalization", later published in CACM as "Understanding deep learning (still) requires rethinking generalization") trained standard CNNs on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet with the labels replaced by random labels. The networks reached zero training error, though more slowly. They also fit images replaced by random noise. Explicit regularizers (weight decay, dropout, data augmentation) neither were necessary for generalization on real labels nor prevented fitting random ones. The lesson is that the hypothesis class (these architectures) contains functions that fit pure noise, so uniform capacity-based bounds over the class cannot explain why the one solution SGD finds on real data generalizes. Any explanation must be data- and algorithm-dependent. They also showed a depth-two network with 2n+d2n+d2n+d parameters can fit any labelling of nnn points in ddd dimensions (a finite-sample expressivity result).

You can reproduce the effect at miniature scale. I trained a single-hidden-layer tanh network (512 units, plain gradient descent on logistic loss) on 200 points in 20 dimensions, whose true labels depend on two coordinates, with an increasing fraction of the labels randomized, and evaluated on fresh clean data.

What has been proposed since. (1) Norm- and margin-based bounds (Bartlett, Foster and Telgarsky, 2017, spectrally-normalized margin bounds) replace parameter count with products of layer norms; they are better than parameter counting but still loose or even increase with data on some tasks (Nagarajan and Kolter 2019 argued that uniform-convergence bounds may be inherently unable to explain deep-network generalization). (2) PAC-Bayes bounds (Dziugaite and Roy, 2017) computed non-vacuous bounds for small networks by optimizing a posterior over weights; the flatness of the found solution matters. (3) Compression bounds (Arora et al., 2018): if a trained network can be compressed to far fewer parameters with little change in output, it generalizes as if it had that smaller count. (4) Algorithmic stability (Hardt, Recht and Singer, 2016): SGD run for few steps on a smooth loss is stable, so generalizes. (5) Benign overfitting (Bartlett, Long, Lugosi and Tsigler, 2020): in linear regression one can interpolate noisy training labels and still have near-optimal test error when the data has many low-variance directions to absorb the noise. All are partial; there is no accepted complete explanation.

Implicit regularization

When there are many global minima of the training loss, the optimizer chooses among them, and its choice is a regularizer nobody wrote down. The cleanest example is overparameterized linear regression.

Gradient descent finds the minimum-norm interpolant

Let X∈Rn×pX\in\R^{n\times p}X∈Rn×p with p>np>np>n and full row rank, and y∈Rn\boldsymbol{y}\in\R^ny∈Rn. Run gradient descent on L(w)=12∥Xw−y∥22\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{w})=\tfrac12\norm{X\boldsymbol{w}-\boldsymbol{y}}_2^2L(w)=21​∥Xw−y∥22​ from w0=0\boldsymbol{w}_0=\boldsymbol{0}w0​=0. Each update is wt+1=wt−ηX⊤(Xwt−y)\boldsymbol{w}_{t+1}=\boldsymbol{w}_t-\eta X^\top(X\boldsymbol{w}_t-\boldsymbol{y})wt+1​=wt​−ηX⊤(Xwt​−y), so by induction wt\boldsymbol{w}_twt​ always lies in the row space of XXX: wt=X⊤at\boldsymbol{w}_t=X^\top\boldsymbol{a}_twt​=X⊤at​ for some at\boldsymbol{a}_tat​. If it converges to a point with Xw∞=yX\boldsymbol{w}_\infty=\boldsymbol{y}Xw∞​=y, then w∞=X⊤a\boldsymbol{w}_\infty=X^\top\boldsymbol{a}w∞​=X⊤a and XX⊤a=yXX^\top\boldsymbol{a}=\boldsymbol{y}XX⊤a=y, so a=(XX⊤)−1y\boldsymbol{a}=(XX^\top)^{-1}\boldsymbol{y}a=(XX⊤)−1y and w∞=X⊤(XX⊤)−1y=X+y,\boldsymbol{w}_\infty=X^\top(XX^\top)^{-1}\boldsymbol{y}=X^{+}\boldsymbol{y},w∞​=X⊤(XX⊤)−1y=X+y, the Moore-Penrose solution, which is the interpolating solution with the smallest ℓ2\ell_2ℓ2​ norm (any other interpolant differs by a vector in the null space of XXX, orthogonal to the row space, and adds norm). No explicit penalty was used.

Other results of this kind: on separable data with logistic or cross-entropy loss, gradient descent drives ∥w∥→∞\norm{\boldsymbol{w}}\to\infty∥w∥→∞ while the direction converges to the maximum-margin SVM solution (Soudry, Hoffer, Nacson, Gunasekar and Srebro, 2018), which explains why test error can keep improving after training error reaches zero. In matrix factorization with small initialization, gradient descent is biased toward low nuclear norm or low rank (Gunasekar et al., 2017; Arora et al., 2019: deeper factorizations are biased more strongly toward low rank). The initialization scale changes the bias, from a "rich" feature-learning regime to a "kernel" regime (Woodworth et al., 2020). SGD noise is thought to prefer flat minima (Keskar et al. 2017; but flatness is not reparameterization-invariant, Dinh et al. 2017), and the edge of stability phenomenon (Cohen et al., 2021: full-batch GD's sharpness rises until 2/η2/\eta2/η and hovers) shows that large-step training dynamics self-regulate in ways classical analyses do not capture. Whether implicit regularization explains the generalization of real deep networks is still unproven; it explains toy models well.

Neural tangent kernel and lazy training

Consider a network f(x;θ)f(\boldsymbol{x};\boldsymbol{\theta})f(x;θ) with parameters θ∈Rp\boldsymbol{\theta}\in\R^pθ∈Rp. Gradient flow on the squared loss over training set {(xi,yi)}\{(\boldsymbol{x}_i,y_i)\}{(xi​,yi​)} changes the function by ddtf(x;θt)=∇θf(x)⊤θ˙t=−∑i=1n∇θf(x)⊤∇θf(xi)⏟Θt(x,xi) (f(xi)−yi),\frac{d}{dt}f(\boldsymbol{x};\boldsymbol{\theta}_t)=\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}f(\boldsymbol{x})^\top\dot{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_t=-\sum_{i=1}^n\underbrace{\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}f(\boldsymbol{x})^\top\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}f(\boldsymbol{x}_i)}_{\Theta_t(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{x}_i)}\,\big(f(\boldsymbol{x}_i)-y_i\big),dtd​f(x;θt​)=∇θ​f(x)⊤θ˙t​=−i=1∑n​Θt​(x,xi​)∇θ​f(x)⊤∇θ​f(xi​)​​(f(xi​)−yi​), so the function evolves according to the neural tangent kernel Θt(x,x′)=⟨∇θf(x;θt),∇θf(x′;θt)⟩\Theta_t(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{x}')=\langle\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}f(\boldsymbol{x};\boldsymbol{\theta}_t),\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}f(\boldsymbol{x}';\boldsymbol{\theta}_t)\rangleΘt​(x,x′)=⟨∇θ​f(x;θt​),∇θ​f(x′;θt​)⟩. In general this kernel changes during training, which is why training is hard to analyze. Jacot, Gabriel and Hongler (NeurIPS 2018) proved that for fully connected networks in the infinite-width limit (with the NTK parameterization, 1/width1/\sqrt{\text{width}}1/width​ output scaling), the kernel at initialization converges to a deterministic limit Θ∞\Theta_\inftyΘ∞​ and stays constant during training. Then fff evolves like kernel regression:

ft(x)=f0(x)−Θ∞(x,X) Θ∞(X,X)−1(I−e−η Θ∞(X,X) t)(f0(X)−y),f_t(\boldsymbol{x})=f_0(\boldsymbol{x})-\Theta_\infty(\boldsymbol{x},X)\,\Theta_\infty(X,X)^{-1}\big(I-e^{-\eta\,\Theta_\infty(X,X)\,t}\big)\big(f_0(X)-\boldsymbol{y}\big),ft​(x)=f0​(x)−Θ∞​(x,X)Θ∞​(X,X)−1(I−e−ηΘ∞​(X,X)t)(f0​(X)−y),

a closed form (with f0(X)f_0(X)f0​(X) the vector of initial outputs on the training set). Consequences: (i) convergence to zero training loss at a linear rate whose speed is the smallest eigenvalue of the kernel matrix Θ∞(X,X)\Theta_\infty(X,X)Θ∞​(X,X) (this is the idea behind global-convergence proofs for overparameterized networks, Du et al. 2019; Allen-Zhu, Li and Song 2019), and (ii) the trained network is equivalent to a kernel machine with a fixed kernel.

Lazy-training sketch. Why does the kernel freeze? Chizat, Oyallon and Bach (2019) gave a general explanation: if the output is scaled by a large factor α\alphaα, fα=α (f(θ)−f(θ0))f_\alpha=\alpha\,(f(\boldsymbol{\theta})-f(\boldsymbol{\theta}_0))fα​=α(f(θ)−f(θ0​)), the loss gradient w.r.t. θ\boldsymbol{\theta}θ is multiplied by α\alphaα, so achieving a fixed change of the output needs only a parameter change of order 1/α1/\alpha1/α. The parameters stay close to θ0\boldsymbol{\theta}_0θ0​, and the network is well approximated by its first-order Taylor expansion f(x;θ)≈f(x;θ0)+∇θf(x;θ0)⊤(θ−θ0)f(\boldsymbol{x};\boldsymbol{\theta})\approx f(\boldsymbol{x};\boldsymbol{\theta}_0)+\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}f(\boldsymbol{x};\boldsymbol{\theta}_0)^\top(\boldsymbol{\theta}-\boldsymbol{\theta}_0)f(x;θ)≈f(x;θ0​)+∇θ​f(x;θ0​)⊤(θ−θ0​), a model that is linear in the parameters with fixed features ∇θf(⋅;θ0)\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}f(\cdot;\boldsymbol{\theta}_0)∇θ​f(⋅;θ0​). That is exactly kernel regression with the tangent kernel. The features never move, so the network never learns representations: it is "lazy".

pythonntk_empirical.py
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
from torch.func import functional_call, vmap, jacrev

torch.manual_seed(0)
net = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(2, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 1))
params = {k: v.detach() for k, v in net.named_parameters()}


def f_single(p, x):
    return functional_call(net, p, (x.unsqueeze(0),)).squeeze()      # scalar output


def empirical_ntk(x1, x2):
    """Theta(x1, x2)_{ab} = <grad_theta f(x1_a), grad_theta f(x2_b)>, shape (n1, n2)."""
    j1 = vmap(jacrev(f_single), (None, 0))(params, x1)               # dict name -> (n1, *param_shape)
    j2 = vmap(jacrev(f_single), (None, 0))(params, x2)
    k = 0.0
    for name in params:
        a, b = j1[name].flatten(1), j2[name].flatten(1)
        k = k + a @ b.T
    return k


x = torch.randn(8, 2)
K = empirical_ntk(x, x)
print(K.shape, torch.allclose(K, K.T, atol=1e-4))
print("eigenvalues:", torch.linalg.eigvalsh(K))     # PSD; smallest eigenvalue controls the convergence rate

What the NTK does not explain: the kernel regime does not match the performance of practical networks, which do change their features (finite-width networks beat their NTK counterpart on CIFAR-10 by large margins, Arora et al. 2019, "On exact computation with an infinitely wide neural net"), so the NTK is a theory of one regime, not of deep learning. The competing view is the mean-field and feature-learning regime (Mei, Montanari and Nguyen 2018; Yang and Hu 2021, maximal-update parameterization, μ\muμP), where hidden representations evolve and hyperparameters (such as learning rate) transfer across widths, an idea with direct practical value for scaling models.

The lottery ticket hypothesis

Pruning (see Week 16) can remove 90% or more of a trained network's weights with little loss, yet training the pruned architecture from a fresh random initialization usually works poorly. Frankle and Carbin (ICLR 2019, "The lottery ticket hypothesis") asked why, and proposed: a randomly initialized dense network contains a sparse subnetwork (a "winning ticket") that, when trained in isolation from its original initialization, matches the full network's test accuracy in a comparable number of iterations.

The procedure to find tickets is iterative magnitude pruning (IMP) with rewinding: (1) initialize θ0\boldsymbol{\theta}_0θ0​, (2) train to get θT\boldsymbol{\theta}_TθT​, (3) remove the smallest-magnitude p%p\%p% of weights to define a binary mask m\boldsymbol{m}m, (4) reset the surviving weights to their values in θ0\boldsymbol{\theta}_0θ0​ and train the masked network m⊙θ0\boldsymbol{m}\odot\boldsymbol{\theta}_0m⊙θ0​, (5) repeat. Tickets for small networks (MNIST fully connected, small CIFAR convnets) were found at 1-10% of the original size. For deeper networks (ResNet-50, VGG on ImageNet), resetting to the exact initialization fails, but late rewinding works: reset to the weights from a very early training iteration kkk (Frankle, Dziugaite, Roy and Carbin, 2020, linear mode connectivity and the lottery ticket hypothesis): the network has by then become stable to SGD noise, meaning that two runs from that point with different data order end up in the same linearly connected basin.

pythonimp.py
import copy
import torch
import torch.nn as nn


def make_masks(model):
    return {n: torch.ones_like(p) for n, p in model.named_parameters() if p.dim() > 1}   # prune weights, not biases


def apply_masks(model, masks):
    with torch.no_grad():
        for n, p in model.named_parameters():
            if n in masks:
                p.mul_(masks[n])


def prune_global(model, masks, frac):
    """Remove the `frac` smallest-magnitude surviving weights (global threshold across layers)."""
    alive = torch.cat([p.detach().abs()[masks[n].bool()].flatten() for n, p in model.named_parameters() if n in masks])
    k = int(frac * alive.numel())
    if k == 0:
        return masks
    thresh = alive.kthvalue(k).values
    return {n: (masks[n].bool() & (p.detach().abs() > thresh)).float() for n, p in model.named_parameters() if n in masks}


def lottery_ticket(model_fn, train_fn, rounds=5, frac=0.2, rewind_state=None):
    """Iterative magnitude pruning with rewinding. train_fn(model, masks) trains the model in place
    (and must re-apply the masks after every optimizer step so pruned weights stay zero)."""
    model = model_fn()
    init_state = copy.deepcopy(model.state_dict()) if rewind_state is None else rewind_state
    masks = make_masks(model)
    for r in range(rounds):
        train_fn(model, masks)
        masks = prune_global(model, masks, frac)
        model.load_state_dict(init_state)          # rewind surviving weights to initialization (or an early iterate)
        apply_masks(model, masks)
        sparsity = 1 - sum(m.sum() for m in masks.values()) / sum(m.numel() for m in masks.values())
        print(f"round {r}: sparsity {sparsity:.1%}")
    return model, masks

The hypothesis is a statement about trainability of sparse networks, not about better final accuracy. It connects pruning, initialization and optimization, and led to "pruning at initialization" methods (SNIP, GraSP, SynFlow), which on careful inspection often do no better than layer-wise random pruning at the same sparsity (Frankle et al. 2021). A practical takeaway is that sparse training from scratch is feasible, but the theory of which connections matter and why is still open.

Grokking

Power et al. (2022, "Grokking: generalization beyond overfitting on small algorithmic datasets") trained small transformers on modular arithmetic tables (e.g. a+b mod 97a+b \bmod 97a+bmod97) with a fraction of the table as training data. Training accuracy reached 100% quickly, while validation accuracy stayed near chance for a long time, then rose suddenly to near 100%, thousands of steps after the training loss was already almost zero. This delayed generalization is grokking.

Subsequent work gave a partial, mechanistic account. Nanda et al. (2023, "Progress measures for grokking via mechanistic interpretability") reverse-engineered a one-layer transformer trained on modular addition and found that it learns to represent the inputs as points on a circle using discrete Fourier features, and implements addition via trigonometric identities (cos⁡(a+b)=cos⁡acos⁡b−sin⁡asin⁡b\cos(a+b)=\cos a\cos b-\sin a\sin bcos(a+b)=cosacosb−sinasinb). Training has three phases: memorization (fit the training set), circuit formation (the generalizing algorithm gradually forms while memorization still dominates the loss), and cleanup (weight decay removes the memorizing components, and test accuracy jumps). The key insight is that a smooth, hidden process underlies the apparent sudden transition, and that weight decay (which favours low-norm, hence more efficient, circuits) drives it. Liu, Michaud and Tegmark (2022) argued grokking requires an initialization and weight norm in a "Goldilocks zone", and Varma et al. (2023) explained grokking in terms of the relative efficiency of memorizing and generalizing circuits. The practical lesson: a flat validation curve with zero training loss is not proof that generalization is impossible, and conversely, reaching zero training loss is the beginning of a representation-learning process, not its end.

Double descent

The classical U-shaped bias-variance curve says test error falls and then rises as model complexity grows. Belkin, Hsu, Ma and Mandal (PNAS 2019, "Reconciling modern machine-learning practice and the classical bias-variance trade-off") observed that if you keep increasing capacity beyond the interpolation threshold, where the model first can fit the training set exactly, test error falls again. Nakkiran et al. (ICLR 2020, "Deep double descent") showed the effect in CNNs, ResNets and transformers, as a function of model size, training epochs, and data size ("epoch-wise" and "sample-wise" double descent: more data can hurt near the threshold).

The cleanest way to see it is minimum-norm least squares with random features. I fit n=40n=40n=40 noisy training points with the first ppp of 400 Gaussian features (noise variance 0.25), using the minimum-norm solution pinv(A) @ y and measuring mean-squared test error averaged over 60 random datasets.

Why the peak? The role of the smallest singular value

For p≥np\ge np≥n the min-norm interpolant is w^=A+y\hat{\boldsymbol{w}}=A^{+}\boldsymbol{y}w^=A+y with A∈Rn×pA\in\R^{n\times p}A∈Rn×p the training feature matrix. Noise ε\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}ε in y\boldsymbol{y}y is mapped through A+A^+A+, so it contributes A+εA^{+}\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}A+ε to w^\hat{\boldsymbol{w}}w^, whose squared norm is at most ∥ε∥2/σmin⁡(A)2\norm{\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}}^2/\sigma_{\min}(A)^2∥ε∥2/σmin​(A)2. At p=np=np=n, a square random matrix has a smallest singular value that is close to zero, so the noise is amplified enormously: the variance diverges. For p≫np\gg np≫n, σmin⁡(A)≈p−n\sigma_{\min}(A)\approx\sqrt p-\sqrt nσmin​(A)≈p​−n​ grows, and the minimum-norm solution spreads the fit over many weak directions, so the variance term shrinks again. Test error is a sum of a bias term (falls with ppp) and this variance term (peaks at p=np=np=n then decays).

Three cautions. Double descent is about interpolation with noise, so it is most visible with label noise or weak regularization. Proper regularization (optimal ridge, early stopping) smooths the peak away (Nakkiran et al., 2021, "Optimal regularization can mitigate double descent"). And the second descent shows that bigger models can generalize better, but it does not say that they always do; the right claim is that classical capacity measures fail, not that complexity is free.

Putting the pieces together

Zhang et al. say capacity measures cannot explain generalization; implicit regularization says SGD plus parameterization picks a particular solution; the NTK says in one limit the picture is kernel regression; the lottery ticket says trainability concentrates in sparse subnetworks; grokking says representation-learning can continue after training loss vanishes; double descent says the classical U-curve is only part of a picture that includes interpolation. A unified theory is missing, and good research problems for MS students are available at the boundary of each.

Open problems and research directions

Predictions about the future are unreliable, so this section lists open questions, each with enough context to find the literature. Treat it as a map of where a project could contribute.

  • Reasoning. Language models solve many reasoning benchmarks, particularly with chain-of-thought prompting (Wei et al., 2022) and training on verifiable rewards, and still fail in ways that look unlike human errors: sensitivity to irrelevant changes, poor out-of-distribution length generalization, inconsistent answers. Open questions: how much of the reasoning in a chain of thought causally drives the answer (faithfulness of explanations, Turpin et al. 2023), how to train and verify long multi-step reasoning without a reliable ground truth, and whether current architectures can represent the needed algorithms (transformers have known expressivity limits at fixed depth, Merrill and Sabharwal 2023).
  • Agents. Models that act in environments (browsing, coding, operating software) over many steps compound errors, are exposed to prompt injection from the content they read, and are hard to evaluate (long horizons, non-deterministic outcomes). Open: reliability over long horizons, safe tool use and sandboxing, measuring autonomy-related risk, credit assignment over very long trajectories, and cost.
  • Data efficiency. Humans learn language from orders of magnitude fewer tokens than large language models. Scaling laws (Kaplan et al. 2020; Hoffmann et al. 2022) describe how loss falls with data and compute, and the supply of high-quality text is finite. Directions: better data curation and curricula, synthetic data and its risks (model collapse when training on one's own outputs, Shumailov et al. 2024), self-supervised objectives that extract more per example, few-shot and in-context adaptation, active learning, and inductive biases.
  • Continual learning. Networks forget earlier tasks when trained on new ones (catastrophic forgetting; McCloskey and Cohen, 1989). Approaches are regularization (EWC, Kirkpatrick et al. 2017), replay, architectural expansion, and parameter-efficient modules. Open: a method that learns indefinitely from a stream, without storing all data, scaling to foundation models, and with a benchmark that reflects deployment (where distribution shift is gradual and unlabeled).
  • World models. A model that predicts how an environment evolves given actions can support planning, imagination and sample-efficient control (Ha and Schmidhuber 2018; the Dreamer family; JEPA-style latent prediction proposed by LeCun, 2022; video generation models used as simulators). Open: whether learned predictors capture causal and physical structure rather than correlations, how to evaluate "understanding", long-horizon consistency, and how to plan in the latent space reliably.
  • Cross-cutting. Reliable evaluation (contamination, benchmark saturation, measuring capabilities and risks), scalable oversight (supervising systems that may exceed our ability to check), alignment and its theory, interpretability that scales to frontier models, efficiency and the energy cost of training (see Week 16), and the science of why all of the above works (the previous section).
Choosing a research problem

A good project has a measurable claim, a baseline that is not a straw man, an ablation that isolates the cause, and an honest account of failure cases. Many of the best contributions in this field are careful negative results and evaluation papers: the sanity checks for saliency maps, the adaptive attacks on defenses, the retrospective on calibration, and the randomization test are all of that kind.

Lab: attack, defend, explain and calibrate

In this lab you will take one small CNN on MNIST through the whole chapter: train a standard model, break it with FGSM and PGD, harden it with adversarial training, explain predictions with Grad-CAM and saliency, and measure and repair its calibration. Everything runs in a few minutes on a Colab GPU (CPU is fine but slower). Run the cells in order; each part reuses the previous variables. We use MNIST so you can see everything; the same code works for CIFAR-10 with a bigger network and ϵ=8/255\epsilon=8/255ϵ=8/255.

Part 0: data and model

pythonlab_setup.py
import torch, torch.nn as nn, torch.nn.functional as F
import torchvision, torchvision.transforms as T
from torch.utils.data import DataLoader, random_split

device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"
torch.manual_seed(0)

# No normalization transform: keep pixels in [0, 1] so that epsilon is in pixel units
tfm = T.ToTensor()
full = torchvision.datasets.MNIST("data", train=True, download=True, transform=tfm)
test = torchvision.datasets.MNIST("data", train=False, download=True, transform=tfm)
train, val = random_split(full, [50000, 10000], generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed(0))   # val is for calibration
train_dl = DataLoader(train, batch_size=128, shuffle=True)
val_dl = DataLoader(val, batch_size=1000)
test_dl = DataLoader(test, batch_size=1000)


class SmallCNN(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.conv1 = nn.Conv2d(1, 32, 3, padding=1)
        self.conv2 = nn.Conv2d(32, 64, 3, padding=1)
        self.fc1 = nn.Linear(64 * 7 * 7, 128)
        self.fc2 = nn.Linear(128, 10)

    def forward(self, x):                                   # x: (B, 1, 28, 28)
        x = F.max_pool2d(F.relu(self.conv1(x)), 2)          # (B, 32, 14, 14)
        x = F.max_pool2d(F.relu(self.conv2(x)), 2)          # (B, 64, 7, 7)  <- last conv features (for Grad-CAM)
        x = F.relu(self.fc1(x.flatten(1)))
        return self.fc2(x)                                  # logits (B, 10)


def train_standard(model, epochs=3, lr=1e-3):
    opt = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=lr)
    for ep in range(epochs):
        model.train()
        for x, y in train_dl:
            x, y = x.to(device), y.to(device)
            loss = F.cross_entropy(model(x), y)
            opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()
        print(f"epoch {ep}: clean test acc {accuracy(model, test_dl):.4f}")


@torch.no_grad()
def accuracy(model, dl):
    model.eval()
    c = n = 0
    for x, y in dl:
        x, y = x.to(device), y.to(device)
        c += (model(x).argmax(1) == y).sum().item(); n += len(y)
    return c / n


std_model = SmallCNN().to(device)
train_standard(std_model)

Expected: clean test accuracy around 0.99 after three epochs.

Part 1: attacks

Reuse fgsm and pgd from the earlier code block (save them in attacks.py, or paste them into a cell), then sweep ϵ\epsilonϵ.

pythonlab_attacks.py
from attacks import fgsm, pgd          # the functions defined in the "Adversarial examples" section

def robust_acc(model, dl, attack, **kw):
    model.eval()
    c = n = 0
    for x, y in dl:
        x, y = x.to(device), y.to(device)
        xa = attack(model, x, y, **kw)                       # needs gradients, computed inside
        with torch.no_grad():
            c += (model(xa).argmax(1) == y).sum().item(); n += len(y)
    return c / n

eps_list = [0.0, 0.05, 0.1, 0.15, 0.2, 0.3]
print("eps   FGSM    PGD-20")
for eps in eps_list:
    a_f = robust_acc(std_model, test_dl, fgsm, eps=eps)
    a_p = robust_acc(std_model, test_dl, pgd, eps=eps, alpha=eps / 8 if eps > 0 else 0.0, steps=20)
    print(f"{eps:.2f}  {a_f:.4f}  {a_p:.4f}")

You should see FGSM accuracy dropping steeply by ϵ=0.1\epsilon=0.1ϵ=0.1 to 0.20.20.2 and PGD driving the standard model to near 0% by ϵ≈0.2\epsilon\approx0.2ϵ≈0.2 (PGD is always at least as strong as FGSM, up to the randomness of the start). A perturbation of 0.30.30.3 on MNIST is large and visible; ϵ≤0.1\epsilon\le0.1ϵ≤0.1 is nearly invisible.

pythonlab_visualize.py
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

x, y = next(iter(test_dl)); x, y = x[:8].to(device), y[:8].to(device)
xa = pgd(std_model, x, y, eps=0.15, alpha=0.02, steps=20)
with torch.no_grad():
    pa, pb = std_model(x).softmax(1), std_model(xa).softmax(1)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(3, 8, figsize=(14, 5.5))
for i in range(8):
    ax[0, i].imshow(x[i, 0].cpu(), cmap="gray"); ax[0, i].set_title(f"{pa[i].argmax().item()} ({pa[i].max():.2f})")
    ax[1, i].imshow((xa - x)[i, 0].cpu(), cmap="RdBu", vmin=-0.15, vmax=0.15); ax[1, i].set_title("perturbation")
    ax[2, i].imshow(xa[i, 0].cpu(), cmap="gray"); ax[2, i].set_title(f"{pb[i].argmax().item()} ({pb[i].max():.2f})")
    for r in range(3): ax[r, i].axis("off")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

Part 2: adversarial training and evaluation

pythonlab_advtrain.py
from adv_train import adversarial_epoch

adv_model = SmallCNN().to(device)
opt = torch.optim.Adam(adv_model.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
for ep in range(5):
    loss, acc_adv = adversarial_epoch(adv_model, train_dl, opt, eps=0.1, alpha=0.025, steps=7, device=device)
    print(f"epoch {ep}: adv-train loss {loss:.3f}  adv-train acc {acc_adv:.3f}  "
          f"clean test {accuracy(adv_model, test_dl):.4f}  PGD-20 test {robust_acc(adv_model, test_dl, pgd, eps=0.1, alpha=0.0125, steps=20):.4f}")

# Compare the two models under identical attacks (eps = 0.1)
for name, m in [("standard", std_model), ("adversarially trained", adv_model)]:
    print(name,
          "clean", round(accuracy(m, test_dl), 4),
          "FGSM", round(robust_acc(m, test_dl, fgsm, eps=0.1), 4),
          "PGD-20", round(robust_acc(m, test_dl, pgd, eps=0.1, alpha=0.0125, steps=20), 4))

Expect the adversarially trained model to keep roughly 90% or more of its accuracy under ϵ=0.1\epsilon=0.1ϵ=0.1 PGD (the exact numbers vary with seed and training length) at the price of a little clean accuracy. Sanity checks you should run yourself: (a) evaluate the adversarially trained model at ϵ=0.3\epsilon=0.3ϵ=0.3 and see that robustness is specific to the training radius; (b) check that PGD with more steps or restarts does not reduce accuracy much more (if it does, the evaluation was too weak); (c) try an ℓ2\ell_2ℓ2​ attack with pgd_l2 to see that ℓ∞\ell_\inftyℓ∞​ training does not guarantee ℓ2\ell_2ℓ2​ robustness.

Part 3: explanations with Grad-CAM and saliency

pythonlab_explain.py
from gradcam import GradCAM               # from the Grad-CAM section; here layer = the second conv layer (7x7 after pooling)
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# The conv layer outputs 14x14 before the final max-pool; hook the module whose output is the 7x7 feature map.
# Easiest: wrap the pooled features as a module.
class Pool(nn.Module):
    def forward(self, x): return F.max_pool2d(x, 2)

class CNNWithPool(SmallCNN):                      # same weights, but the pooled map is an explicit module
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__(); self.pool = Pool()
    def forward(self, x):
        x = self.pool(F.relu(self.conv1(x)))
        x = self.pool(F.relu(self.conv2(x)))
        return self.fc2(F.relu(self.fc1(x.flatten(1))))

def with_pool(model):
    m = CNNWithPool().to(device); m.load_state_dict(model.state_dict()); return m.eval()

m_std, m_adv = with_pool(std_model), with_pool(adv_model)
x, y = next(iter(test_dl)); x, y = x[:6].to(device), y[:6].to(device)

def saliency(model, x, cls):
    x = x.clone().requires_grad_(True)
    score = model(x).gather(1, cls.view(-1, 1)).sum()
    g, = torch.autograd.grad(score, x)
    return g.abs().squeeze(1)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(4, 6, figsize=(12, 8))
for name_i, (name, m) in enumerate([("standard", m_std), ("adv-trained", m_adv)]):
    cam_fn = GradCAM(m, m.pool)       # note: m.pool is called twice; the hook fires twice and keeps the LAST output (7x7)
    cam, cls = cam_fn(x)
    sal = saliency(m, x, cls)
    for i in range(6):
        ax[2 * name_i, i].imshow(sal[i].detach().cpu(), cmap="magma"); ax[2 * name_i, i].set_title(f"{name} saliency")
        ax[2 * name_i + 1, i].imshow(x[i, 0].cpu(), cmap="gray"); ax[2 * name_i + 1, i].imshow(cam[i].cpu(), cmap="jet", alpha=0.45)
        ax[2 * name_i + 1, i].set_title(f"{name} Grad-CAM")
        ax[2 * name_i, i].axis("off"); ax[2 * name_i + 1, i].axis("off")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

# Randomization sanity check: Grad-CAM from a model with re-initialized final layer should look different
m_rand = with_pool(std_model); nn.init.normal_(m_rand.fc2.weight, std=0.1)
cam_r, _ = GradCAM(m_rand, m_rand.pool)(x, cls)
print("mean |difference| after randomizing the classifier layer:", (cam_r.cpu() - cam.cpu()).abs().mean().item())

What to look for: the saliency map of the adversarially trained model is typically much cleaner and more digit-shaped than the standard model's noisy map (Tsipras et al. 2019 and Kaur et al. 2019 observed that robust models have more perceptually aligned gradients), which is a nice by-product, though it does not mean the standard model is "wrong". Grad-CAM at 7×77\times77×7 resolution is blobby on MNIST because the digits are small relative to the grid, a useful reminder that its resolution is limited.

Part 4: measure and repair calibration

pythonlab_calibration.py
from calibration import reliability_bins, fit_temperature

@torch.no_grad()
def collect_logits(model, dl):
    model.eval(); L, Y = [], []
    for x, y in dl:
        L.append(model(x.to(device)).cpu()); Y.append(y)
    return torch.cat(L), torch.cat(Y)

for name, m in [("standard", std_model), ("adv-trained", adv_model)]:
    Lv, Yv = collect_logits(m, val_dl); Lt, Yt = collect_logits(m, test_dl)
    ece_before = reliability_bins(Lt.softmax(1), Yt)[1]
    T = fit_temperature(Lv, Yv)                       # fit on validation, evaluate on test
    ece_after = reliability_bins((Lt / T).softmax(1), Yt)[1]
    nll_b = F.cross_entropy(Lt, Yt).item(); nll_a = F.cross_entropy(Lt / T, Yt).item()
    print(f"{name:12s}  T = {T:.2f}  ECE {ece_before:.4f} -> {ece_after:.4f}  NLL {nll_b:.4f} -> {nll_a:.4f}")

# Confidence of the standard model on an OOD input (Fashion-MNIST) vs MNIST: MSP and energy
fm = torchvision.datasets.FashionMNIST("data", train=False, download=True, transform=tfm)
Lo, _ = collect_logits(std_model, DataLoader(fm, batch_size=1000))
Li, _ = collect_logits(std_model, test_dl)
from ood_scores import msp_score, energy_score, auroc
print("AUROC MSP   :", auroc(msp_score(Li), msp_score(Lo)))
print("AUROC energy:", auroc(energy_score(Li), energy_score(Lo)))

Deliverables for the lab report: (1) the table of clean, FGSM and PGD accuracy for both models; (2) one figure of clean, perturbed and perturbation images with predictions; (3) the saliency and Grad-CAM figure with a paragraph interpreting differences, including the randomization check; (4) reliability diagrams and ECE/NLL before and after temperature scaling for both models, plus one sentence on whether adversarial training changes calibration; (5) the OOD AUROC for MSP versus energy.

Exercises

Exercise 1: FGSM for a linear model (derivation)

For a logistic regression p(y=1∣x)=σ(w⊤x+b)p(y=1\mid\boldsymbol{x})=\sigma(\boldsymbol{w}^\top\boldsymbol{x}+b)p(y=1∣x)=σ(w⊤x+b) with label y∈{0,1}y\in\{0,1\}y∈{0,1} and cross-entropy loss, (a) compute ∇xL\nabla_{\boldsymbol{x}}\mathcal{L}∇x​L, (b) give the FGSM adversarial example, and (c) show that the logit moves by exactly ϵ∥w∥1\epsilon\norm{\boldsymbol{w}}_1ϵ∥w∥1​ in the direction that hurts, when x\boldsymbol{x}x is correctly classified.

Solution

(a) L=−ylog⁡p−(1−y)log⁡(1−p)\mathcal{L}=-y\log p-(1-y)\log(1-p)L=−ylogp−(1−y)log(1−p) with p=σ(z)p=\sigma(z)p=σ(z), z=w⊤x+bz=\boldsymbol{w}^\top\boldsymbol{x}+bz=w⊤x+b. Then ∂L/∂z=p−y\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial z=p-y∂L/∂z=p−y and ∇xL=(p−y)w\nabla_{\boldsymbol{x}}\mathcal{L}=(p-y)\boldsymbol{w}∇x​L=(p−y)w. (b) xadv=x+ϵ sign((p−y)w)\boldsymbol{x}_{\text{adv}}=\boldsymbol{x}+\epsilon\,\mathrm{sign}\big((p-y)\boldsymbol{w}\big)xadv​=x+ϵsign((p−y)w). If y=1y=1y=1 then p−y<0p-y<0p−y<0, so the step is −ϵ sign(w)-\epsilon\,\mathrm{sign}(\boldsymbol{w})−ϵsign(w); if y=0y=0y=0, p−y>0p-y>0p−y>0 and it is +ϵ sign(w)+\epsilon\,\mathrm{sign}(\boldsymbol{w})+ϵsign(w). (c) For y=1y=1y=1: zadv=z−ϵ w⊤sign(w)=z−ϵ∑i∣wi∣=z−ϵ∥w∥1z_{\text{adv}}=z-\epsilon\,\boldsymbol{w}^\top\mathrm{sign}(\boldsymbol{w})=z-\epsilon\sum_i\abs{w_i}=z-\epsilon\norm{\boldsymbol{w}}_1zadv​=z−ϵw⊤sign(w)=z−ϵ∑i​∣wi​∣=z−ϵ∥w∥1​. The classifier flips when z<ϵ∥w∥1z<\epsilon\norm{\boldsymbol{w}}_1z<ϵ∥w∥1​, i.e. for ϵ>z/∥w∥1\epsilon>z/\norm{\boldsymbol{w}}_1ϵ>z/∥w∥1​: the margin in units of the ℓ1\ell_1ℓ1​-norm of the weights decides robustness. Note: for the linear model FGSM is exactly optimal for the ℓ∞\ell_\inftyℓ∞​ ball (the loss is monotone in the logit).

Exercise 2: Dimension dependence (conceptual and coding)

In the chart earlier, the same per-coordinate budget ϵ\epsilonϵ is more damaging in higher dimension. (a) Show that with w\boldsymbol{w}w having all entries of magnitude mmm, the logit change under an ℓ∞\ell_\inftyℓ∞​ attack is ϵmd\epsilon m dϵmd but under random sign noise it is about ϵmd\epsilon m\sqrt dϵmd​ in standard deviation. (b) Write NumPy code to verify numerically for d=10,100,1000d=10,100,1000d=10,100,1000.

Solution

(a) The attack: w⊤δ=ϵ∑im=ϵmd\boldsymbol{w}^\top\boldsymbol{\delta}=\epsilon\sum_i m=\epsilon m dw⊤δ=ϵ∑i​m=ϵmd. Random: δ=ϵs\boldsymbol{\delta}=\epsilon\boldsymbol{s}δ=ϵs with independent signs si=±1s_i=\pm1si​=±1, so w⊤δ=ϵm∑isi′\boldsymbol{w}^\top\boldsymbol{\delta}=\epsilon m\sum_is'_iw⊤δ=ϵm∑i​si′​ with mean 0 and variance ϵ2m2d\epsilon^2m^2dϵ2m2d, so the standard deviation is ϵmd\epsilon m\sqrt dϵmd​. The ratio of attack to noise effect is d\sqrt dd​. (b)

python
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
for d in [10, 100, 1000]:
    w = np.full(d, 0.5); eps = 0.01
    attack = w @ (eps * np.sign(w))
    noise = np.std([w @ (eps * rng.choice([-1, 1], d)) for _ in range(5000)])
    print(d, attack, noise, attack / noise)    # ratio is close to sqrt(d)
Exercise 3: PGD versus FGSM (what would happen if...)

You evaluate a defended model and find FGSM accuracy 62% and PGD-20 accuracy 41% at the same ϵ\epsilonϵ. Then you find that a black-box transfer attack from an undefended surrogate gives 30% accuracy on it. What do you conclude, and what do you do next?

Solution

FGSM above PGD is normal (PGD is stronger). The red flag is that a transfer attack beats the white-box attack (30% < 41%): a gradient-based white-box attack should be at least as strong as one crafted on a different model. That points to gradient masking or an under-powered attack (too few steps, a badly chosen step size, a saturating loss, non-differentiable preprocessing). Next: use more steps and restarts, switch to a margin loss instead of cross-entropy, run AutoAttack, use BPDA/EOT if the defense has non-differentiable or randomized parts, and check that accuracy goes to 0% at very large ϵ\epsilonϵ. Until then, report the strongest number (30% or lower), not the PGD number.

Exercise 4: Temperature scaling preserves accuracy (derivation and coding)

(a) Prove that dividing logits by T>0T>0T>0 never changes the argmax. (b) Show that the NLL of softmax⁡(z/T)\softmax(\boldsymbol{z}/T)softmax(z/T) on a dataset is a convex function of β=1/T\beta=1/Tβ=1/T. (c) Write a PyTorch snippet fitting TTT by L-BFGS on validation logits.

Solution

(a) zj/T>zk/T  ⟺  zj>zkz_j/T>z_k/T\iff z_j>z_kzj​/T>zk​/T⟺zj​>zk​ for T>0T>0T>0, so the ordering is unchanged. (b) NLL(β)=1n∑i[log⁡∑jeβzij−βziyi]\mathrm{NLL}(\beta)=\frac1n\sum_i\big[\log\sum_je^{\beta z_{ij}}-\beta z_{iy_i}\big]NLL(β)=n1​∑i​[log∑j​eβzij​−βziyi​​]. The log-sum-exp of a linear function of β\betaβ is convex, and −βziyi-\beta z_{iy_i}−βziyi​​ is linear, so the sum is convex in β\betaβ. (c)

python
import torch, torch.nn.functional as F
def fit_T_lbfgs(logits, labels):
    beta = torch.ones(1, requires_grad=True)                    # beta = 1/T
    opt = torch.optim.LBFGS([beta], lr=0.1, max_iter=100)
    def closure():
        opt.zero_grad()
        loss = F.cross_entropy(logits * beta, labels)
        loss.backward()
        return loss
    opt.step(closure)
    return (1 / beta).item()

Because the loss is convex in β\betaβ the optimizer finds the global optimum; optimizing 1/T1/T1/T (or log⁡T\log TlogT) is better conditioned than optimizing TTT directly.

Exercise 5: Conformal coverage by hand (coding)

With a calibration set of n=19n=19n=19 scores and α=0.1\alpha=0.1α=0.1, which order statistic is used as q^\hat qq^​? Then simulate 20,000 trials to confirm the coverage lies between 0.90.90.9 and 0.9+1/(n+1)=0.950.9+1/(n+1)=0.950.9+1/(n+1)=0.95.

Solution

k=⌈(n+1)(1−α)⌉=⌈20×0.9⌉=18k=\lceil(n+1)(1-\alpha)\rceil=\lceil20\times0.9\rceil=18k=⌈(n+1)(1−α)⌉=⌈20×0.9⌉=18, so q^\hat qq^​ is the 18th smallest of the 19 scores. The guarantee gives coverage between 18/20=0.9018/20=0.9018/20=0.90 and 0.900.900.90 here (since k/(n+1)=0.9k/(n+1)=0.9k/(n+1)=0.9 exactly), so coverage is exactly 0.90.90.9 for continuous scores.

python
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n, alpha, trials = 19, 0.1, 20000
k = int(np.ceil((n + 1) * (1 - alpha)))
cov = np.mean([rng.random() <= np.sort(rng.random(n))[k - 1] for _ in range(trials)])
print(k, cov)       # ~0.90
Exercise 6: Integrated Gradients completeness (challenging)

(a) Prove completeness from the fundamental theorem of calculus. (b) For F(x)=ReLU⁡(x1) x2F(\boldsymbol{x})=\relu(x_1)\,x_2F(x)=ReLU(x1​)x2​ with baseline 0\boldsymbol{0}0 and input (2,3)(2,3)(2,3), compute IG analytically and verify the sum. (c) Compute the plain gradient at (2,3)(2,3)(2,3) and at the point (−1,3)(-1,3)(−1,3), and explain what IG does better.

Solution

(a) See the derivation in the text: F(x)−F(x′)=∫01ddtF(x′+t(x−x′))dt=∑i(xi−xi′)∫01∂iF dtF(\boldsymbol{x})-F(\boldsymbol{x}')=\int_0^1\frac{d}{dt}F(\boldsymbol{x}'+t(\boldsymbol{x}-\boldsymbol{x}'))dt=\sum_i(x_i-x'_i)\int_0^1\partial_iF\,dtF(x)−F(x′)=∫01​dtd​F(x′+t(x−x′))dt=∑i​(xi​−xi′​)∫01​∂i​Fdt. (b) Path x(t)=(2t,3t)\boldsymbol{x}(t)=(2t,3t)x(t)=(2t,3t). F=ReLU⁡(2t)⋅3t=6t2F=\relu(2t)\cdot3t=6t^2F=ReLU(2t)⋅3t=6t2. ∂1F=1[x1>0] x2=3t\partial_1F=\ind[x_1>0]\,x_2=3t∂1​F=1[x1​>0]x2​=3t, ∂2F=ReLU⁡(x1)=2t\partial_2F=\relu(x_1)=2t∂2​F=ReLU(x1​)=2t. IG1=2∫013t dt=2⋅1.5=3\mathrm{IG}_1=2\int_0^13t\,dt=2\cdot1.5=3IG1​=2∫01​3tdt=2⋅1.5=3; IG2=3∫012t dt=3\mathrm{IG}_2=3\int_0^12t\,dt=3IG2​=3∫01​2tdt=3. Sum =6=F(2,3)−F(0,0)=6=6=F(2,3)-F(0,0)=6=6=F(2,3)−F(0,0)=6. ✓. (c) At (2,3)(2,3)(2,3) the gradient is (3,2)(3,2)(3,2), which multiplied by the input gives (6,6)(6,6)(6,6) for gradient-times-input, summing to 12, double-counting the interaction (the output is 6). At (−1,3)(-1,3)(−1,3): F=0F=0F=0 and the gradient is (0,0)(0,0)(0,0) (ReLU inactive), so plain gradient says no feature matters, whereas IG integrates over the path from the baseline: here F≡0F\equiv0F≡0 along the path so IG is also 0, correctly (the output does not change). IG's gain appears in saturating cases such as F=min⁡(x,1)F=\min(x,1)F=min(x,1) at x=5x=5x=5: gradient 0, IG=1=1=1.

Exercise 7: Fairness criteria (derivation and numbers)

Group A has base rate 0.5, group B has base rate 0.2. A classifier has FNR =0.2=0.2=0.2 and PPV =0.8=0.8=0.8 in both groups. (a) Compute the FPR in each group using the identity from the text. (b) Does equalized odds hold? (c) Which criterion would you equalize for a screening tool whose positive prediction triggers an invasive follow-up? Argue.

Solution

(a) FPR=p1−p⋅1−PPVPPV⋅(1−FNR)\mathrm{FPR}=\frac{p}{1-p}\cdot\frac{1-\mathrm{PPV}}{\mathrm{PPV}}\cdot(1-\mathrm{FNR})FPR=1−pp​⋅PPV1−PPV​⋅(1−FNR). Group A: 0.50.5⋅0.20.8⋅0.8=0.20\frac{0.5}{0.5}\cdot\frac{0.2}{0.8}\cdot0.8=0.200.50.5​⋅0.80.2​⋅0.8=0.20. Group B: 0.20.8⋅0.25⋅0.8=0.05\frac{0.2}{0.8}\cdot0.25\cdot0.8=0.050.80.2​⋅0.25⋅0.8=0.05. (b) FNR equal (0.2) but FPR differs (0.20 versus 0.05): equalized odds fails although predictive parity holds. Forcing equal FPR would require either dropping PPV in one group or changing FNR. (c) An invasive follow-up makes false positives costly, which argues for equalizing the FPR (and for high PPV) so that healthy members of any group are equally unlikely to be subjected to it; one could still set the thresholds separately by group, subject to the legal and ethical context. There is no universally right answer, and the stakeholder discussion is part of the deliverable.

Exercise 8: DP-SGD noise scale (derivation and design)

A DP-SGD run uses clip norm C=1C=1C=1, noise multiplier σ=1.1\sigma=1.1σ=1.1, expected batch size B=256B=256B=256, in a model with p=106p=10^6p=106 parameters. (a) What is the standard deviation of the noise per coordinate of the averaged gradient, and the expected norm of the total noise vector? (b) If a typical clipped per-example gradient has norm about 0.50.50.5, estimate the norm of the averaged signal at best (all gradients aligned). (c) What do you change to improve the signal-to-noise ratio? List three levers and a downside for each.

Solution

(a) Noise on the sum has std σC=1.1\sigma C=1.1σC=1.1 per coordinate; after dividing by BBB, std =1.1/256≈0.0043=1.1/256\approx0.0043=1.1/256≈0.0043. The noise vector norm is about 0.0043106=4.30.0043\sqrt{10^6}=4.30.0043106​=4.3. (b) If all per-example gradients are aligned the average has norm 0.50.50.5 at most (realistically much less, since gradients disagree). So the noise norm (4.3) can exceed the signal by an order of magnitude; progress is possible only because the signal accumulates across steps while the noise averages out, and because gradients live in a low-dimensional subspace. (c) Levers: larger batch size (noise ∝1/B\propto1/B∝1/B; downside: fewer steps per epoch or a bigger privacy cost per step as qqq grows, and compute); smaller σ\sigmaσ (less noise; downside: larger ε\varepsilonε); fewer parameters, for example fine-tune an adapter or last layer of a pretrained model (noise norm ∝p\propto\sqrt p∝p​; downside: lower capacity); tuning the clip norm CCC (reduces bias when CCC is near the median gradient norm; downside: it needs tuning, and a too-large CCC means more noise relative to the signal).

Consider the linearized model flin(x;θ)=f(x;θ0)+∇θf(x;θ0)⊤(θ−θ0)f_{\text{lin}}(\boldsymbol{x};\boldsymbol{\theta})=f(\boldsymbol{x};\boldsymbol{\theta}_0)+\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}f(\boldsymbol{x};\boldsymbol{\theta}_0)^\top(\boldsymbol{\theta}-\boldsymbol{\theta}_0)flin​(x;θ)=f(x;θ0​)+∇θ​f(x;θ0​)⊤(θ−θ0​) trained by gradient flow on squared loss. (a) Show that the loss is convex in θ\boldsymbol{\theta}θ. (b) Derive the trajectory of the training-set predictions u(t)=flin(X;θt)\boldsymbol{u}(t)=f_{\text{lin}}(X;\boldsymbol{\theta}_t)u(t)=flin​(X;θt​) and show u(t)−y=e−tK(u(0)−y)\boldsymbol{u}(t)-\boldsymbol{y}=e^{-t K}(\boldsymbol{u}(0)-\boldsymbol{y})u(t)−y=e−tK(u(0)−y), where K=JJ⊤K=JJ^\topK=JJ⊤ with J=∇θf(X;θ0)∈Rn×pJ=\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}f(X;\boldsymbol{\theta}_0)\in\R^{n\times p}J=∇θ​f(X;θ0​)∈Rn×p. (c) What does the smallest eigenvalue of KKK say about the rate?

Solution

(a) flinf_{\text{lin}}flin​ is affine in θ\boldsymbol{\theta}θ, so L=12∥u−y∥2\mathcal{L}=\frac12\norm{\boldsymbol{u}-\boldsymbol{y}}^2L=21​∥u−y∥2 is a convex quadratic in θ\boldsymbol{\theta}θ. (b) With u=u0+J(θ−θ0)\boldsymbol{u}=\boldsymbol{u}_0+J(\boldsymbol{\theta}-\boldsymbol{\theta}_0)u=u0​+J(θ−θ0​), gradient flow gives θ˙=−J⊤(u−y)\dot{\boldsymbol{\theta}}=-J^\top(\boldsymbol{u}-\boldsymbol{y})θ˙=−J⊤(u−y), so u˙=Jθ˙=−JJ⊤(u−y)=−K(u−y)\dot{\boldsymbol{u}}=J\dot{\boldsymbol{\theta}}=-JJ^\top(\boldsymbol{u}-\boldsymbol{y})=-K(\boldsymbol{u}-\boldsymbol{y})u˙=Jθ˙=−JJ⊤(u−y)=−K(u−y), a linear ODE with solution u(t)−y=e−tK(u(0)−y)\boldsymbol{u}(t)-\boldsymbol{y}=e^{-tK}(\boldsymbol{u}(0)-\boldsymbol{y})u(t)−y=e−tK(u(0)−y). (c) In the eigenbasis of KKK the residual component along eigenvector vk\boldsymbol{v}_kvk​ decays as e−λkte^{-\lambda_kt}e−λk​t. The slowest component decays with λmin⁡\lambda_{\min}λmin​, so training time to reach a tolerance scales like 1/λmin⁡1/\lambda_{\min}1/λmin​; if λmin⁡=0\lambda_{\min}=0λmin​=0 (e.g., duplicated or too few features, p<np<np<n), exact interpolation is impossible. This is the core of global convergence proofs for wide networks: show that KKK stays positive definite near initialization.

Exercise 10: Design a trustworthiness audit (open-ended)

You are handed a CNN that classifies chest X-rays for pneumonia, trained at Hospital A, to be deployed at Hospital B. Draft a one-page audit plan that covers: distribution shift, calibration, subgroup performance, explanations, privacy of the training data, and the model card. Name at least one concrete test, one metric and one acceptance criterion for each.

Solution

One reasonable plan. Shift: collect an unlabeled sample from B, train a domain classifier (AUROC near 0.5 means little covariate shift), compare ID/OOD scores (energy), label a small B sample to measure accuracy; criterion: accuracy drop under 3 points or a recalibration/fine-tuning plan. Calibration: reliability diagram and ECE on labelled B data before and after temperature scaling on a B validation split; criterion: ECE below 0.03 and an abstention rule at a confidence threshold. Subgroups: TPR/FPR by sex, age band, scanner model, and intersections, with bootstrap confidence intervals; criterion: TPR gap below an agreed threshold, and no group with TPR below a clinical minimum. Explanations: Grad-CAM on a stratified sample read by a radiologist plus a randomization sanity check and a deletion curve; look for shortcut cues (text markers, tubes, scanner artefacts). Privacy: loss-threshold and LiRA membership tests against held-out patients; consider DP fine-tuning; criterion: attack TPR at 1% FPR close to chance. Model card: intended use, exclusion criteria (paediatric patients?), disaggregated metrics, known failures, monitoring and update plan, and who to contact. Add post-deployment drift monitoring.

Common mistakes and debugging tips

Symptom Likely cause Fix
Adversarial attack does nothing (accuracy unchanged) Model in train() mode with dropout, attack gradient is zero because the logits saturate, or input not in requires_grad model.eval(), use logits-based margin loss, x.requires_grad_(True), check grad.abs().max()
Adversarial examples exceed the budget Forgot projection, or clipping to [0,1][0,1][0,1] happens before adding the perturbation Project onto ϵ\epsilonϵ-ball and clamp to the valid range after every step
Epsilon is "8/255" but inputs were normalized by mean/std Perturbation is applied in normalized space Attack in pixel space, normalize inside the model (a first layer), or rescale ϵ\epsilonϵ by the std
Robust accuracy 0% at small ϵ\epsilonϵ after "adversarial training" Catastrophic overfitting of single-step training, or training on perturbations of a stale model Use PGD, random start, early stopping on a PGD validation set
"Defense" works against FGSM but not PGD, or black-box beats white-box Gradient masking Adaptive attacks, AutoAttack, check unbounded-ϵ\epsilonϵ attack reaches 0%
Evaluating robustness on the same samples used for attack tuning Leaks into hyperparameters Hold out an attack-evaluation split
ECE looks great but the model is useless Always predicting base rates, or too few samples per bin Report accuracy, NLL, Brier; use equal-mass bins; bootstrap
Temperature fitted on the test set Optimistic calibration numbers Fit on a validation split; evaluate on test
Calibration collapses after deployment Distribution shift Monitor ECE on a labelled sample; ensembles; recalibrate per domain
MSP OOD detector flags everything or nothing Threshold chosen on one OOD set; detector given softmax of a different temperature Fix a threshold from ID data only (e.g. 95% TPR) and test on several OOD sets
Saliency map looks nice but is unchanged after randomizing weights The method (e.g. guided backprop) is mostly edge detection Run the Adebayo et al. sanity checks; add deletion/insertion curves
Grad-CAM highlights the wrong region or is empty Wrong layer, gradients of softmax instead of logit, or all-ReLU-negative CAM Use the last conv layer, class logit, and check cam.max() before normalizing
IG attributions do not sum to F(x)−F(x′)F(x)-F(x')F(x)−F(x′) Too few steps, or baseline mismatch Increase steps; verify completeness
Probe gets 95% accuracy on random-init network Probe too powerful or label leakage via input Linear probe, control task, selectivity
Group metrics based on tiny subgroups swing wildly High variance Confidence intervals; combine with other evidence; collect more data
DP-SGD training diverges or accuracy is near chance Clip norm too small/large, noise too high, tiny batch Tune CCC near the median gradient norm, increase batch size, use pretrained features
Reported ε\varepsilonε cannot be trusted Sampling without replacement or fixed-size batches while the accountant assumes Poisson; reused data across steps in ways the accountant ignores Use the library's data loader; document the accountant and assumptions
Conformal sets have under-coverage in deployment Exchangeability violated (shift), calibration data used in training Recalibrate on recent data; use weighted/adaptive conformal methods; keep calibration disjoint
A default workflow for evaluating trustworthiness

(1) Accuracy on in-distribution and shifted/corrupted data; (2) calibration (ECE, NLL, reliability diagram) and a rule for abstention; (3) robustness under a named threat model with an adaptive attack; (4) subgroup metrics with confidence intervals; (5) explanations validated by sanity checks and interventions; (6) a privacy review of what the model could reveal; (7) a model card. Skipping steps is fine if you say that you skipped them.

Key takeaways

Key takeaways
  • Adversarial examples come from maximizing the loss in a small perturbation set. FGSM is the exact first-order solution for ℓ∞\ell_\inftyℓ∞​ (ϵ sign(∇xL)\epsilon\,\mathrm{sign}(\nabla_{\boldsymbol{x}}\mathcal{L})ϵsign(∇x​L)); PGD iterates it with projection and is the standard evaluation. High dimension plus near-linearity makes small perturbations powerful.
  • A threat model (goal, capability, knowledge, setting) is part of every robustness claim. Evaluate with adaptive attacks; gradient masking is the usual reason for a false sense of security.
  • Adversarial training (a min-max problem) is the strongest empirical defense, costing about (K+1)×(K+1)\times(K+1)× compute and some clean accuracy. Certified defenses (IBP, Lipschitz, randomized smoothing) give provable but smaller radii.
  • Distribution shift (covariate, label, concept) is the norm; OOD detectors (MSP, energy, Mahalanobis) are useful but not universal.
  • Uncertainty: aleatoric (irreducible) versus epistemic (reducible, disagreement among models). Deep ensembles are the strongest simple method; MC dropout is a cheap approximation. Calibration is measured by reliability diagrams and ECE and often fixed with a single temperature, which does not change accuracy.
  • Conformal prediction wraps any model to give sets with marginal coverage ≥1−α\ge1-\alpha≥1−α under exchangeability, with a short proof; the guarantee is marginal, not conditional.
  • Explanations: gradients are local and noisy; SmoothGrad averages; Grad-CAM weights feature maps by pooled gradients; Integrated Gradients satisfies completeness and sensitivity but depends on the baseline. Attention is not an explanation, and a probe shows decodability, not use. Validate with sanity checks and interventions. Mechanistic interpretability seeks causal circuits; superposition and sparse autoencoders are central ideas.
  • Fairness criteria (demographic parity, equalized odds, predictive parity) conflict when base rates differ; choosing among them is a normative decision. Audit with disaggregated metrics.
  • Privacy: models leak membership and training data; (ε,δ)(\varepsilon,\delta)(ε,δ)-DP bounds that leakage; DP-SGD clips per-example gradients and adds Gaussian noise, at a cost in accuracy that falls hardest on rare groups.
  • Responsible release means model cards, red-teaming, staged access and monitoring. Documentation is only valuable if it contains uncomfortable numbers.
  • Theory: deep networks fit random labels yet generalize (Zhang et al.), so capacity-based bounds fail; SGD has implicit biases (minimum norm, max margin); the NTK describes a lazy regime; lottery tickets, grokking and double descent each show that training dynamics matter. No unified theory exists.
  • Open problems (reasoning, agents, data efficiency, continual learning, world models) are mostly questions of evaluation and reliability as much as of capability.

Further reading

Essential (marked with a star) and supporting references. Check the venue or arXiv listing for the latest version.

Robustness and adversarial examples

  • (Essential) Goodfellow, Shlens, Szegedy. Explaining and Harnessing Adversarial Examples. ICLR 2015 (arXiv:1412.6572).
  • Szegedy et al. Intriguing properties of neural networks. ICLR 2014 (arXiv:1312.6199).
  • (Essential) Madry, Makelov, Schmidt, Tsipras, Vladu. Towards Deep Learning Models Resistant to Adversarial Attacks. ICLR 2018 (arXiv:1706.06083).
  • Athalye, Carlini, Wagner. Obfuscated Gradients Give a False Sense of Security. ICML 2018.
  • Cohen, Rosenfeld, Kolter. Certified Adversarial Robustness via Randomized Smoothing. ICML 2019.
  • Ilyas et al. Adversarial Examples Are Not Bugs, They Are Features. NeurIPS 2019.
  • Croce and Hein. Reliable evaluation of adversarial robustness with an ensemble of diverse parameter-free attacks (AutoAttack). ICML 2020.
  • Zhang et al. Theoretically Principled Trade-off between Robustness and Accuracy (TRADES). ICML 2019.

Shift and uncertainty

  • Hendrycks and Gimpel. A Baseline for Detecting Misclassified and Out-of-Distribution Examples in Neural Networks. ICLR 2017.
  • Liu, Wang, Owens, Li. Energy-based Out-of-distribution Detection. NeurIPS 2020.
  • Lee, Lee, Lee, Shin. A Simple Unified Framework for Detecting Out-of-Distribution Samples and Adversarial Attacks. NeurIPS 2018.
  • Lakshminarayanan, Pritzel, Blundell. Simple and Scalable Predictive Uncertainty Estimation using Deep Ensembles. NeurIPS 2017.
  • Gal and Ghahramani. Dropout as a Bayesian Approximation. ICML 2016.
  • (Essential) Guo, Pleiss, Sun, Weinberger. On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks. ICML 2017.
  • Ovadia et al. Can You Trust Your Model's Uncertainty? Evaluating Predictive Uncertainty Under Dataset Shift. NeurIPS 2019.
  • Angelopoulos and Bates. A Gentle Introduction to Conformal Prediction and Distribution-Free Uncertainty Quantification. 2021 (arXiv:2107.07511).

Interpretability

  • (Essential) Selvaraju et al. Grad-CAM: Visual Explanations from Deep Networks via Gradient-based Localization. ICCV 2017.
  • Sundararajan, Taly, Yan. Axiomatic Attribution for Deep Networks. ICML 2017.
  • Smilkov et al. SmoothGrad: removing noise by adding noise. 2017 (arXiv:1706.03825).
  • Adebayo et al. Sanity Checks for Saliency Maps. NeurIPS 2018.
  • Jain and Wallace. Attention is not Explanation. NAACL 2019; Wiegreffe and Pinter. Attention is not not Explanation. EMNLP 2019.
  • Hewitt and Liang. Designing and Interpreting Probes with Control Tasks. EMNLP 2019.
  • Elhage et al. A Mathematical Framework for Transformer Circuits. Transformer Circuits Thread, 2021; Toy Models of Superposition, 2022.
  • Bricken et al. Towards Monosemanticity: Decomposing Language Models With Dictionary Learning. Transformer Circuits Thread, 2023.

Fairness, privacy, safety

  • Hardt, Price, Srebro. Equality of Opportunity in Supervised Learning. NeurIPS 2016.
  • Kleinberg, Mullainathan, Raghavan. Inherent Trade-Offs in the Fair Determination of Risk Scores. ITCS 2017; Chouldechova. Fair prediction with disparate impact. Big Data 2017.
  • Barocas, Hardt, Narayanan. Fairness and Machine Learning: Limitations and Opportunities. MIT Press, 2023 (free online).
  • Buolamwini and Gebru. Gender Shades. FAT* 2018.
  • Shokri, Stronati, Song, Shmatikov. Membership Inference Attacks Against Machine Learning Models. IEEE S&P 2017.
  • Dwork and Roth. The Algorithmic Foundations of Differential Privacy. 2014.
  • (Essential) Abadi et al. Deep Learning with Differential Privacy. CCS 2016.
  • Mitchell et al. Model Cards for Model Reporting. FAT* 2019; Gebru et al. Datasheets for Datasets. CACM 2021.

Theory

  • (Essential) Zhang, Bengio, Hardt, Recht, Vinyals. Understanding deep learning requires rethinking generalization. ICLR 2017.
  • Jacot, Gabriel, Hongler. Neural Tangent Kernel: Convergence and Generalization in Neural Networks. NeurIPS 2018.
  • Chizat, Oyallon, Bach. On Lazy Training in Differentiable Programming. NeurIPS 2019.
  • (Essential) Frankle and Carbin. The Lottery Ticket Hypothesis: Finding Sparse, Trainable Neural Networks. ICLR 2019.
  • Belkin, Hsu, Ma, Mandal. Reconciling modern machine-learning practice and the classical bias-variance trade-off. PNAS 2019.
  • Nakkiran et al. Deep Double Descent. ICLR 2020.
